text: summary A multirotor has no control surfaces: all control is changing motor RPM. This module explains how four six, eight propellers produce throttle, roll, pitch and yaw, why the props spin in opposite directions, what the mixer is, and why the thrust-to-weight ratio defines a drone's character. This is the foundation that PIDs, filters and all of tuning stand on. theory Thrust and weight A propeller throws air down and gets thrust up. To hover, the total thrust of all motors must equal the weight. Thrust grows roughly as the square of RPM: to double the thrust you need to raise RPM by about 1.4×. The thrust-to-weight ratio T/W is the maximum thrust of all motors divided by the takeoff weight: - around 2:1 — the minimum for controllable flight: heavy platforms, cargo octocopters; - 3:1–4:1 — calm long-range 7–10" builds; - 6:1 and above — freestyle and racing. At a 2:1 T/W, hover is at about half throttle, and there is almost no margin for maneuvering or a gust of wind. That's the main argument for why you can't tune a heavy drone like a five-inch. {{diagram:chart-hover-throttle Газ висения лежит между долей тяги f и квадратом: при T/W 4.1 это 24–49 %, по кривой 0.65 — 40 %; 60 % газа — уже T/W 2.25–2.8, для 5–7" это стоп.}} Reaction torque and spin directions A motor spinning up a prop simultaneously tries to turn the frame the opposite way — that's reaction torque. If all props spun the same way, the frame would rotate about the vertical axis. So a quadcopter has two pairs: diagonal props spin one way, neighboring props the opposite way. The torques cancel out as long as the RPMs are equal. {{diagram:quad-forces Quadcopter roll and yaw: a thrust difference gives a moment about an axis, a difference in the reaction torques of the CCW/CW pairs gives yaw.}} The four control axes - Throttle: all motors faster or slower at the same time. - Roll: the motors on one side faster, on the other side slower. Roll right — the left motors speed up. - Pitch: front against rear. Nose down flying forward — the rear motors speed up. - Yaw: the diagonal pairs. A motor spinning counterclockwise pushes the frame clockwise. To turn clockwise viewed from above , the counterclockwise-spinning motors are sped up and the other pair slowed down. Total thrust barely changes. Yaw is the “weakest” axis: the torque from an RPM difference is small compared with the moments from a thrust difference. So in yaw the drone responds more slowly and hits the motor limits more easily. The mixer The flight controller computes the desired throttle, roll, pitch and yaw, and the mixer turns them into a command for each motor. For each motor it is a sum: throttle plus the roll, pitch and yaw contributions, with a sign that depends on the motor's position and spin direction. The mixer is set by the frame type Quad X, Hex, Octo X8, etc. , and the firmware knows the signs for each type. Hence the main rule: the motor order and spin directions in the firmware must match the real build. A swapped motor means a drone that flips over instantly on takeoff. Motor saturation If some motor is already at 100% or 0%, the mixer can't fully execute the command. Firmwares handle this differently Betaflight — air mode and mixer scaling, ArduPilot — roll/pitch priority over yaw , but you can't cheat physics: no thrust margin, no control. The mixer in numbers Quad X, Betaflight convention Motor command = throttle + k_r·roll + k_p·pitch + k_y·yaw, where each k is ±1 depending on position and spin direction. For Quad X Betaflight numbering: 1 — rear right, 2 — front right, 3 — rear left, 4 — front left; “props in”/“props out” flips the yaw signs : Motor roll pitch yaw --- --- --- --- 1 rear right CW −1 +1 −1 2 front right CCW −1 −1 +1 3 rear left CCW +1 +1 +1 4 front left CW +1 −1 −1 the yaw signs depend on the firmware's convention; ArduPilot uses its own numbering around the circle — always check against the frame type diagram . Example: throttle 0.5, roll command +0.1, everything else 0 → motors 1,2 = 0.4, motors 3,4 = 0.6: more thrust on the left — roll right. Yaw command +0.05 → 1 = 0.45, 2 = 0.55, 3 = 0.55, 4 = 0.45: the total thrust is the same, the reaction torques no longer cancel → the frame turns. Why yaw is weak — an estimate Roll/pitch moment = Δthrust × lever arm 0.1–0.3 m : with Δ = 200 g 2 N and a 0.15 m arm — 0.3 N·m. Yaw moment = the difference in the motors' reaction torques: a motor's reaction torque ≈ power/angular velocity = 150 W / 14,000 rpm ≈ 1470 rad/s ≈ 0.1 N·m; a 30% change on a pair — ~0.06 N·m. 5 times less — hence the slow yaw and the quick hit into saturation. With “props out” and tilted motors part of the thrust works on yaw — faster, but with losses. Dynamics: from command to angle Angular acceleration = moment / moment of inertia J for a 5", J in roll ≈ 0.003–0.005 kg·m²; for a 15" X8 — 50–100 times more : 0.3 N·m / 0.004 = 75 rad/s² ≈ 4300 °/s² — that's why a 5" reaches 1000 °/s in a quarter of a second, while an X8 with the same relative thrust margin is an order of magnitude slower, and its PID gains and acceleration limits ATC_ACCEL_ _MAX are different. In detail — the “Flight Mechanics” module. practice Lab: calculate the T/W of your build 1. Find the thrust table for your prop and voltage in the motor's datasheet: the maximum thrust of one motor, g. 2. Multiply by the number of motors — that's the maximum thrust. 3. Weigh the drone with the battery, camera and everything it carries in flight. 4. T/W = maximum thrust / takeoff weight. Write it into the drone's log. 5. Check against a flight log: average hover throttle should be roughly 1 / T/W corrected for nonlinearity — thrust grows faster than throttle . Checking directions without props 1. Remove the props. 2. On the Motors tab Betaflight or in Motor Test ArduPilot , spin each motor in turn at low throttle. 3. Check the number and spin direction against your firmware's frame diagram. text: summary “How a multirotor flies” explained the principle; this module turns it into equations you can calculate with. Hover, climb, bank and turn are four force balances that give you numbers: how much thrust and current each mode needs, how fast the aircraft accelerates at a 30° bank, why a heavy aircraft on long arms is “lazy” moment of inertia and lever arm , and why you have to add throttle in a bank to hold altitude. Everything comes with a calculation for a 7" at 1.4 kg, which you then check against a log. theory Forces: Newton's second law for a drone The forces on the aircraft: weight m·g downward, total thrust T along the aircraft's axis perpendicular to the prop plane , air drag D opposite to the velocity. The equation of motion: m·a = T + m·g + D as vectors . Four modes: 1. Hover. a = 0, thrust is vertical: T = m·g . For 1.4 kg: T = 1.4 × 9.81 = 13.7 N = 1400 gf. Per motor — 350 gf. This is exactly the “hover throttle” you see in the log. 2. Climb. To accelerate upward at a: T = m· g + a + D. Accelerating to 3 m/s in 1 s → a = 3 m/s² → T = 1.4 × 12.8 = 17.9 N 1830 gf, +30% over hover . A steady 3 m/s climb: a = 0, you only need to overcome drag — at that speed D is small ~20 gf with the same C_d = 1.1 and A = 0.03 m² for a 7" , T ≈ m·g + D ≈ 1410–1420 gf. Takeaway: it's the acceleration that's expensive, not the climb rate. But a propeller in an upward flow works worse V₀ in the thrust formula grows , and the real throttle in a climb is higher than this estimate gives. 3. Bank or pitch while holding altitude. The aircraft is tilted by an angle φ, and the thrust tilts with it. The vertical component must equal the weight: T·cos φ = m·g → T = m·g / cos φ . The horizontal component accelerates you: m·a = T·sin φ → a = g·tan φ . - φ = 30°: T = 1.155·m·g +15.5% throttle , a = 5.7 m/s². - φ = 45°: T = 1.41·m·g, a = 9.8 m/s² 1 g . - φ = 60°: T = 2·m·g — a 2:1 T/W is no longer enough to hold altitude. This is why in Angle mode with a 60° tilt limit a drone with a 2:1 T/W sinks in hard maneuvers, and why Betaflight/INAV/ArduPilot have tilt-based throttle compensation e.g. thr_corr_value Betaflight , throttle_tilt_comp_str INAV , ATC_ANGLE_BOOST ArduPilot in various forms . 4. Turn coordinated turn . The centripetal acceleration v²/r comes from the horizontal component of thrust: m·v²/r = m·g·tan φ → r = v² / g·tan φ . 15 m/s at a 30° bank: r = 225 / 5.66 = 40 m. To make a 20 m radius at the same speed you need a 49° bank and throttle ×1.52. Air drag D = ½·ρ·C_d·A·v² , ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, A — frontal area, C_d ≈ 1.0–1.3 for a “box with arms”. A 7" with a frontal area of 0.03 m² at 20 m/s: D = 0.5 × 1.225 × 1.1 × 0.03 × 400 = 8 N — more than half its weight! That's why maximum horizontal speed is limited: at tilt φ the drag is balanced by T·sin φ, and there is no further acceleration. Falling: when D = m·g the aircraft reaches terminal velocity v_t = √ 2·m·g / ρ·C_d·A ; for our example ≈ 26 m/s — the speed at which it hits the ground if all motors fail at a high altitude. Moments: why an aircraft is “snappy” or “lazy” Rotation about an axis is driven by the moment M = ΔT·L : the thrust difference ΔT between opposite motors times the lever arm L distance from the motor to the axis . The angular acceleration is α = M / I , where I is the moment of inertia I = Σ mᵢ·rᵢ² each part's mass times the square of its distance to the axis . - Mass at the arm tips motors, props is expensive: r² grows fast. 4 motors of 35 g on 15 cm arms give I = 4 × 0.035 × 0.15² ≈ 0.0032 kg·m² — the same as a 300 g battery shifted 10 cm from the center. - A big aircraft: the lever arm L grows linearly, I grows quadratically. That's why a 15" X8 with any reasonable thrust rotates slower than a 5": with ΔT = 500 gf on a 0.4 m arm M = 2 N·m, I ≈ 0.3 kg·m² → α ≈ 6.7 rad/s² 380°/s² ; a 5" with M = 0.5 N·m and I = 0.004 → α = 125 rad/s² 7000°/s² . A 20× difference — hence the different PIDs and rates. - Yaw is controlled not by thrust but by the motors' reaction torques the speed difference between the CW and CCW pairs . These torques are small, and I about the vertical axis is the largest all masses are far from the axis , so yaw is the “laziest” axis on every multirotor, especially on big aircraft. This is the reason for the reduced D and large I-term on yaw, and for tilted motors on some frames. Equations as a tool Putting it all together: for any maneuver you can estimate the required thrust → current from the motor's table , the acceleration and the radius. Good practice is a mode table for your own aircraft: hover / climb / 30° bank / 45° bank / max speed — with thrust, current and margin to T_max. A margin below 20% in the heaviest mode means: in a gust or with voltage sag the aircraft will sink. {{diagram:forces-moments Translational motion is set by forces thrust, weight, drag , rotational motion by moments and the inertia J.}} {{diagram:chart-tilt-thrust The thrust needed to hold altitude in a tilt grows as 1/cos φ: at 30° you need +15.5 %, at 60° twice the weight. An aircraft with T/W = 2 physically cannot hold altitude steeper than 60°.}} practice Step 1. Data Mass m with battery scales , lever arm L center → motor axis , the masses of the large parts and their distances to the center, the motor's thrust table thrust → current . Step 2. Mode table For hover, a 3 m/s² upward acceleration, a 30° bank and a 45° bank: T = m·g·k k = 1, 1.31, 1.155, 1.41 , thrust per motor, current from the table, margin to maximum. Step 3. Moments of inertia I for roll/pitch: motors+props at L, battery and FC near the center, the frame roughly as a ring of mass m_frame at a radius of 0.6·L. Record I_roll, I_pitch, I_yaw for yaw all masses are in the horizontal plane: motors at L, battery at the center . Step 4. Check against the log From a hover log: hover throttle and current. text: summary The bridge between “how it flies” and “power circuit design.” Without it, people copy other people's solutions: they add a capacitor because “that's how it's done” and don't understand why the BEC is hot. This module gives you the minimum you need to calculate: Ohm's law, power, series and parallel connections, the thrust → power → current → voltage sag chain in formulas, safe multimeter use and the rules for handling LiPo: charging, storage, damage, fire. theory Three quantities and two formulas - Voltage U volts is the “pressure” in the circuit. A 4S battery is 14.8 V nominal, 16.8 V full. - Current I amps is the “flow.” A 5" motor at full throttle draws 30–40 A. - Resistance R ohms is what impedes the flow. A motor winding is a fraction of an ohm, a wire is milliohms. Ohm's law: U = I·R. If 60 A flows through a resistance of 10 mΩ wire + connector , 0.6 V drops across it. Power P = U·I = I²·R = U²/R watts . The same 60 A through 10 mΩ is 36 W of heat in the wire and connector. That's why current is the main enemy: losses grow with the square of the current. Series and parallel - Series S : voltages add up, the current is shared. 6 cells of 3.7 V = 22.2 V 6S . Resistances add up too. - Parallel P : the current splits, the voltage is shared, capacities add up. 4 cells of 3 Ah = 12 Ah 4P ; the internal resistance is divided by 4. 18650 cells of 3 Ah and 30 mΩ in a 6S4P pack: 22.2 V, 12 Ah, R_int = 30 × 6 / 4 = 45 mΩ. The chain from thrust to sag 1. You need thrust T from mechanics: m·g in hover . 2. From the motor table: thrust → power P_mech and current I_motor at voltage U. 3. Battery current ≈ ΣI_motors + loads ESCs pass current through, they don't multiply it; but at partial throttle the battery current is lower than the motor phase current, because the ESC works as a step-down converter . 4. Sag ΔU = I· R_int_battery + R_wires + R_connectors . Under load U_onboard = U_open-circuit − ΔU. 5. Power delivered by the battery: P = U_onboard·I; losses P_loss = I²·R_total heat the battery and the wires. Example: a 10" heavy-lift, 4 × 5 A = 20 A in hover, R_int of a 6S Li-Ion 4P battery 45 mΩ, wires and XT60 15 mΩ → ΔU = 20 × 0.06 = 1.2 V, losses 24 W. At full throttle 100 A → ΔU = 6 V ! and 600 W of losses: Li-Ion isn't for racing. Energy and capacity Capacity in Ah or mAh is how much current for how many hours. Energy in Wh = Ah × U_nom. 6S 4 Ah = 88.8 Wh. At an average power of 300 W that's 0.3 h = 18 min in theory, ~14 if you use 80%. C rating is the maximum current as a multiple of capacity: 4 Ah × 25C = 100 A. Real values are often lower than the label; look at the sag under load. Multimeter: what and how - Voltage V⎓ : probes in parallel with what you measure; black in COM, red in V. Safe almost always. Battery check: the whole pack and each cell through the balance connector a difference 0.05 V means imbalance . - Continuity • : only on a de-energized circuit. A beep between + and − of the power bus = short circuit. On a circuit with a capacitor the beep may be short and then the resistance rises; that's normal. - Resistance Ω : de-energized. Motor windings give three identical values 0.05–0.3 Ω; a cheap multimeter will show noise, what matters is that they match . A difference means a short between turns. - Current A : probes in series , red in the 10 A jack; above 10 A is off-limits you'll blow the fuse or the meter . The classic beginner mistake: leaving the probe in the A jack and measuring voltage, which is a short circuit through the meter. Onboard current is measured with the FC's current sensor calibrated or with an inline wattmeter. - Diode test : checks diodes and junctions; it'll come in handy later. LiPo: rules that aren't up for discussion - Per-cell voltages: full 4.20 V HV: 4.35 , nominal 3.7, storage 3.80–3.85, minimum under load ~3.3–3.5, below 3.0 means damage. - Charging : only with a balance charger, current ≤ 1C 4 Ah → 4 A unless the manufacturer allows more; in a LiPo bag or on a non-flammable surface; never unattended; don't charge it cold < 5 °C or hot. - Storage : at storage voltage, somewhere cool; don't leave it full for more than a day, or it loses capacity and puffs up. - Damage : puffing, a puncture, a smell: the battery doesn't fly anymore. Discharge it to 0 salt water or a discharger and dispose of it properly. After a drone crash, put the battery in an open, non-flammable spot for 30 minutes. - Fire : a LiPo sustains its own fire and is hard to put out. Plan ahead: a bucket of sand, a place to throw it, don't breathe the smoke. Lots of water cools it and is acceptable for LiPo there's no metallic lithium in it , but the best tool is prevention: correct charging, inspection, a bag. - Short circuit : short-circuit current is hundreds of amps; a connector welds itself in a fraction of a second. Solder the power connector one contact at a time, insulate your tools, don't put an XT60 down on metal. {{diagram:thrust-sag-chain The chain from thrust to sag: more thrust means more current, a bigger drop across the internal resistance and a lower voltage under load.}} practice {{widget:wire-drop}} Step 1. Electrical passport A table: the battery's open-circuit voltage, the voltage of each cell, the 5 V and 9 V BEC outputs with no load and with the electronics connected , the resistance of the three phases of each motor. Step 2. Calculating hover current From the motor table: thrust per motor in hover → current → ×4 + 1 A for the electronics. Write it down. Battery R_int: from the datasheet or measured: U_open-circuit − U under a known load current, divided by that current. Step 3. Cross-check After a hover, get the average current from the log the current sensor must be calibrated against a wattmeter . The discrepancy and its cause go into the passport. Step 4. LiPo checklist Your own one-page checklist: charging, storage, inspection, what to do after a crash, where the sand is. Pin it up at your charging spot. Reference values and a worked example - Li

text: summary The battery is the heaviest and the most dangerous part of a drone. This module explains how LiPo differs from Li-Ion, what “S”, “mAh” and “C” really mean, why voltage sags under load, how to estimate flight time, and how to burn down neither the battery nor the workshop. At the end — a real log from a heavy 10", where the voltage sag told more than any spec sheet. theory Designations - S — the number of cells in series. 6S = 6 cells, the voltages add up. - mAh — capacity. 1300 mAh = 1.3 Ah. - C — discharge current as a multiple of capacity. 1300 mAh × 100C = 130 A according to the label. Marketing C ratings are almost always inflated; go by internal resistance and real tests. - P — parallel cells in packs built from cylindrical cells 6S2P = 12 cells . LiPo vs. Li-Ion - LiPo: nominal 3.7 V/cell, full charge 4.2 V LiHV — 4.35 V . Delivers huge currents, but less energy per gram. For freestyle, racing, anything with high currents and short flights. - Li-Ion 18650, 21700 : nominal around 3.6 V, full 4.2 V, deeper discharge — down to 2.8–3.0 V. Noticeably more energy per gram, more modest currents. For long-range 7–10", wings, long hovers at moderate throttle. Selection rule: if the average current per cell is low long-range flight, a wing , Li-Ion gives more minutes. If you need peaks of tens of amps — LiPo. Voltage sag Every cell has an internal resistance R. Under a current I the voltage drops by I × R. On a sharp throttle punch the sag is instant, and the flight controller sees not “how much is left” but “how much is left minus the sag”. Hence false low-voltage warnings on punches, and real ESC cutouts with a depleted battery. Flight time Estimate: time, min ≈ usable capacity, Ah / average current, A × 60. Usable capacity is about 80% of nominal: never run it down to zero. Take the average current from the log, not out of your head. BEC and onboard voltages The flight controller, receiver, camera and VTX run on 5, 9 or 12 V, not on 6S. These voltages come from BECs — regulators on the flight controller or the ESC. Before connecting peripherals, check: which pad it is powered from, whether the BEC has enough current a VTX at high power can draw more than an amp , and that the VTX is not connected to 5 V if it needs 9–12 V. Case study: voltage sag on a 10" A log from a heavy 10" on 6S battery at 23.8 V at the start of the flight : median current 14–16 A, but p95 on an aggressive profile was 124 A, with a peak of 147 A. At those peaks the voltage dropped to 16.2 V, i.e. 2.7 V per cell. Conclusion: at such currents the battery is working at its limit, and the ESC must be checked for a continuous current of about 125 A. No label would have told you that — the log did. Calculating flight time honestly t ≈ capacity × usable fraction / average current. The fraction: 0.8 for LiPo land at 3.5 V/cell , 0.85 for Li-Ion down to 3.0 V/cell . The average current comes from the log BAT.Curr / amperageLatest , not from hover: a 5" freestyle — 25–40 A average with 60–100 A peaks; a 7" long range cruising — 8–12 A; a 15" X8 hover — 56 A. Example: a 6S 4000 mAh Li-Ion on a 7" at 10 A: 0.85 × 4 / 10 × 60 ≈ 20 min. Check after the flight: the mAh put back by the charger should match CurrTot /mAh drawn in the log within ±10% — otherwise the current sensor is calibrated wrong BATT_AMP_PERVLT , ibata_scale . Voltage sag and internal resistance in numbers U under load = E − I·R. A “fresh” LiPo 6S 1300 mAh 100C: R ≈ 2 mΩ/cell → 12 mΩ/pack; at 80 A the sag is 1 V 4.0 → 3.84 V/cell . The same pack after 150 cycles — 6 mΩ/cell → 36 mΩ → 2.9 V of sag: that's why “old” packs trigger the OSD warning on the very first punch. A Li-Ion 6S4P P42A ≈ 40–50 mΩ/pack: at 60 A — 2.4–3 V, one cell's worth “disappears”; that's why warning thresholds are set by voltage under load or by mAh. Heat: 60 A × 60 A × 0.045 Ω = 160 W in the pack — a Li-Ion heats up noticeably; a 100C LiPo — 80 × 80 × 0.012 = 77 W. In detail chemistries, packs, BMS — the “Li-Ion Packs” module. Charging, storage, disposal Balance charge at 1C LiPo / 0.5–1C Li-Ion , up to 4.2 V/cell 4.1 gives longer life ; storage at 3.8 V/cell LiPo / 3.6–3.7 Li-Ion , no longer than a day at full charge; cell spread after charging ≤ 0.02 V, after a flight ≤ 0.05 — more means a weak cell; per-cell IR in the charger as a “health record”; puffing/puncture — retire it discharge in salt water, dispose of it . In winter: below 10 °C a LiPo loses up to 30–50% of its output — warm it to 20–30 °C before flying. BEC rails: the budget The 5 V sum: FC 0.2 + RX 0.2 + GPS 0.1 + LED 0.5 ≈ 1 A → the board's 5 V/2–3 A BEC is enough; add a Raspberry Pi 2–3 A — not enough, use a separate BEC. 9–12 V: a digital air unit at 0.8–1.2 A → a 9 V/2 A BEC on the FC is cutting it close when it heats up; a separate 3 A BEC is more relaxed. All the numbers go into the build sheet the “Power Circuit Design” module . {{diagram:flight-time-chain An honest flight-time calculation: the usable fraction of capacity, the average current over the whole profile, corrections for conditions.}} {{diagram:chart-discharge Discharge curves: under load a cell sags by I·R, so a LiPo at 40C hits 3.5 V sooner, and a Li-Ion at 3C loses a noticeable part of its capacity before cutoff. The curve shapes are typical, the resistances come from the module's examples.}} practice Handling LiPo safely 1. Charge at 1C, on a non-flammable surface, supervised, with balancing. 2. Storage — around 3.8 V/cell Storage mode on the charger . A full battery sitting on a shelf for weeks degrades and puffs up. 3. A puffed, punctured battery or one with damaged wrap is taken out of service. 4. Transport — in a fireproof bag or box. 5. After a hard crash, set the battery aside and watch it before charging. Lab: calculate flight time and check it against the log 1. Take the battery capacity and the average current from the Blackbox or DataFlash log. 2. text: summary A brushless motor doesn't spin by itself: it is driven by an ESC electronic speed controller , which takes commands from the flight controller. This module explains what numbers like “2207 1750KV” mean, what poles are, why everyone moved from analog PWM to digital DShot, and which ESC firmware is current in 2026 after BLHeli_32 shut down. theory Motor designation - 2207 — stator size: 22 mm diameter, 7 mm height. A bigger stator means more torque. - KV — RPM per volt with no load. 1750KV on 6S 25.2 V is roughly 44,000 rpm without a prop. Less under load. - 12N14P — 12 stator coils, 14 magnets. The number of magnets is motor_poles in the firmware; the RPM filter needs it. Selection rule: a big prop needs a lot of torque and low KV, a small prop needs high KV. A high-KV motor on a big prop overheats and draws a huge current. What the ESC does A brushless motor is three-phase. The ESC energizes the phases in turn, creating a rotating magnetic field. It determines the rotor position without sensors — from the back-EMF induced in the unpowered phase sensorless . Hence desync: on a sharp throttle change the ESC can “lose” the rotor, and the motor stutters or stops. Control protocols - PWM — a 1000–2000 µs pulse at about 50 Hz. Analog, slow, requires range calibration. Still found on servos and heavy-lift ESCs. - OneShot, Multishot — the same pulses, just shorter and more frequent. A historical stage. - DShot150/300/600 — a digital protocol: a 16-bit packet with a checksum, no calibration needed, noise doesn't shift the throttle. The number is the speed in kilobits. - Bidirectional DShot — the ESC replies with the motor's eRPM. The RPM filter is built on this. {{diagram:dshot-frame A DShot frame: 11 throttle bits, a telemetry request bit and 4 CRC bits.}} RPM is calculated from eRPM like this: RPM = eRPM / number of magnets / 2 . ESC firmware in 2026 - BLHeli_S — old 8-bit ESCs, open source. People flash Bluejay onto them — with bidirectional DShot and the RPM filter. - BLHeli_32 — 32-bit ESCs. The project shut down in June 2024: the firmware server is offline, there will be no more updates. Existing ESCs keep working and can still be configured. - AM32 — open firmware for 32-bit ESCs, the de facto replacement for BLHeli_32. Moving from BLHeli_32 to AM32 is one-way. ESC current Choose an ESC by its continuous current rating, with a margin over the real peak current from the log. A 4-in-1 is convenient and light, but overheating one channel often kills the whole board. Motor physics in two formulas A brushless motor is two constants linked to each other: KV rpm per volt and Kt torque per amp . Kt = 60/ 2π·KV N·m/A: a 1750KV motor gives 0.0055 N·m per amp, a 380KV motor 0.025 N·m/A. So low KV = high torque per amp = a big prop without overheating; high KV = RPM for a small prop. RPM under load: n = KV · U − I·R_winding — sag from the winding resistance tens of mΩ and from the battery's internal resistance. Heat in the winding P = I²·R: at 30 A and 40 mΩ — 36 W per motor; the only heatsink is the bell itself and the airflow from the prop. Stator size sets the torque volume of magnetic material : 2207 and 2306 have almost the same volume, and the difference is smaller than between manufacturers. The usual view is that a wider stator 2306 gives slightly more torque and a snappier response, while a taller one 2207 sheds heat better on long flights — compare using the thrust tables of specific motors, not the size numbers. The number of pole pairs 14 magnets = 7 pairs sets the eRPM → RPM conversion and the commutation frequency: at 30,000 rpm, 7 pairs = 3500 electrical revolutions/s. What the ESC does every few microseconds An ESC is a three-phase inverter on 6 MOSFETs. It commutates the phases according to the rotor position, which it estimates from the back-EMF in the unpowered phase zero-crossing . The ESC firmware parameters that matter: - PWM frequency 24/48/96 kHz — the PWM frequency on the switches: higher is quieter and smoother at low throttle, but more switching losses and ESC heating; 48 kHz is the compromise for a 5". - Timing motor timing, 16–24° — commutation advance: higher gives more RPM/power at high RPM, lower gives more reliable sync and runs cooler. - Demag compensation — protection against desync on a sharp throttle chop demagnetization current ; “High” for heavy props. - Startup power / rampup — a smooth start for big props. - Current limit / temperature protection — the ESC reduces power when it overheats: in the log it looks like a “thrust drop”. Desync means the ESC lost the rotor position: the motor stutters, screams, thrust drops; causes — long phase wires, high timing, a prop too big for the KV, old firmware. DShot: how a frame is built 16 bits: 11 bits of value 0 — stop, 1–47 — special commands, 48–2047 — throttle , 1 telemetry request bit, 4 CRC bits. A bit is encoded by pulse width: “1” ≈ 75% of the bit period, “0” ≈ 37%; DShot300 — a 3.33 µs bit, a 53 µs frame; DShot600 — 1.67 µs and 27 µs. A frame is sent every PID loop. Bidirectional DShot : after the frame the line is turned around, and the ESC replies with a frame carrying eRPM the period of an electrical revolution , GCR-encoded; errors in this reply show up as E% on the Motors tab — normal is 0, and at 1–2% the RPM filter places its notches in the wrong spot. Special DShot commands 1–47 : beeper, spin direction reversal dshot_cmd 7/8 — motor direction , 3D on/off, ESC info request — the configurator uses these on the Motors tab. Worked example: matching a motor and prop A 5" freestyle on 6S, 700 g: you need T/W ≥ 5 → 3500 g total, 875 g max per motor. The table for a 2207 1750KV with a 5.1×3 prop: max ~1600 g at 38 A — there's margin; hover ~180 g per motor at ~4 A. A 45 A 4-in-1 ESC — 45 A continuous against a 38 A peak per channel: enough, but “cutting it close” in aggressive flying on a fresh battery; 55–60 A is more relaxed. A 7" long range on 6S at 1.4 kg: 2806.5 1300KV + 7×3.5: max ~1200 g at ~22 A →

text: summary The propeller is the only part that turns electricity into flight, and the only one beginners pick “by the picture.” This module gives you enough physics to choose deliberately: where thrust comes from, why a big slow prop is more efficient than a small fast one, what pitch and efficiency are, how to read a manufacturer's thrust tables and how to match a motor-prop-battery combo to the T/W and flight time you need. With worked calculations for a 7" and an X8. theory Actuator disk: where thrust comes from The simplest model: the prop is a disk of area A that accelerates air from velocity V₀ the incoming flow to Vₑ behind the disk . Thrust is the change in the air's momentum per second: {{diagram:actuator-disk Actuator disk: thrust is the change in the flow's momentum; power grows faster than thrust.}} F = ½ · ρ · A · Vₑ² − V₀² , where ρ is air density ≈1.225 kg/m³ at sea level . In hover V₀ = 0, and thrust grows with the square of the velocity of the air thrown back. Consequences: - A big disk pays off. For the same thrust a big prop throws a lot of air slowly, a small one throws a little air fast. Kinetic energy ~ V², momentum ~ V: at equal thrust the small prop needs more power. That's why long-range and heavy-lift aircraft fly on big slow props. - Air density matters. In the mountains and in the heat ρ is lower, so thrust drops at the same RPM; a drone that barely hovered on the plain won't take off in the mountains. - The model is ideal: real losses tip vortices, blade profile drag, flow swirl reduce efficiency. Pitch, diameter and designation “5×4.3×3” = 5" diameter, 4.3" pitch, 3 blades. Pitch is how far the prop “screws” into the air per revolution with no slip. More pitch means more flow velocity and thrust per revolution, but more torque and current. More blades means more thrust from the same diameter at the cost of efficiency. Dimensionless coefficients Manufacturers and databases UIUC describe a prop with: - Cₜ = T / ρ·n²·D⁴ : thrust coefficient n in rev/s, D is diameter in m ; - Cₚ = P / ρ·n³·D⁵ : power coefficient; - J = V / n·D : advance ratio flight speed relative to prop speed ; - η = J·Cₜ/Cₚ : efficiency in flight in hover J = 0, and people talk about static efficiency in g/W . The practical takeaway from the formulas: thrust ~ n², power ~ n³. To double thrust you need 1.41 times the RPM and 2.8 times the power. That's exactly why “giving it more throttle” costs so much current. Motor + prop: the operating point The motor sets the RPM through KV and voltage, the prop sets the load. The operating point is where motor torque equals the prop's drag torque. Motor manufacturers publish tables: prop, voltage, throttle → thrust g , current A , power W , g/W. That's the main document when choosing. The higher the KV with the same prop, the higher the RPM, thrust and current. Overdo it and you overheat the winding and the ESC. Rule of thumb: big prop, low KV 10": 600–900 KV on 6S ; small prop, high KV 5": 1700–2300 KV on 6S . Hover efficiency Static efficiency in g/W is the key figure for flight time. Typical values: a 5" racer ~4–6 g/W in hover, a 7" ~8–10, 10–15" ~12–20. The higher the g/W, the longer the hover on the same battery. Coaxial pairs and wings In an X8 the lower prop works in the swirled, accelerated flow of the upper one: the total thrust of the pair is less than twice a single prop's losses of 10–20% as a ballpark . On a wing the prop works at J 0, and you have to choose it for cruise speed, not for hover: static efficiency hardly matters there. {{diagram:chart-thrust-current Thrust grows as the square of RPM, current as the cube: at half throttle 375 g at 5 A 3.4 g/W , at full throttle 1500 g at 40 A 1.7 g/W . Model T ∝ n², I ∝ n³; for a real motor use the manufacturer's thrust table.}} practice {{widget:tw-calc}} Step 1. What you need for the calculation 1. Takeoff mass m everything that flies . 2. Target T/W 2:1 heavy-lift, 3–4:1 long-range, 6+:1 freestyle . 3. The thrust table of the candidate motor+prop combos at your voltage. Step 2. Worked example: a 7" at 1.4 kg - Hover thrust needed: 1400 g / 4 motors = 350 g per motor. - T/W 3:1 → 1050 g per motor at maximum. - From the table for a 2806.5 1300KV motor with a 7×3.5 prop on 6S: maximum ~1200 g at ~22 A → it fits. At 350 g it's about 2.5–3 A and ~55–65 W per motor ≈6 g/W; the exact number only comes from your own motor's table . - Hover current: 4 × 3 + 1 A for the electronics = 13 A. A 6S 4000 mAh Li-Ion battery: 0.8 × 4 / 13 × 60 ≈ 15 min of pure hover; with maneuvers and wind, 20–40% less. If that's not enough, go with a 7×4 prop higher g/W on this motor or more capacity, recalculating the weight. Step 3. An X8 on 4008 380KV - Mass 6 kg, eight motors, but coaxial losses ~15%: count the effective thrust of a pair as 1.7 times a single prop. - Needed in hover: 6000 g / 4 pairs × 1.7 ≈ 880 g per motor. - From the table for a 4008 380KV with a 15×5.5 prop on 6S: ~880 g at ~7 A. Hover current ≈ 56 A. Li-Ion 6S 20 Ah → 0.8 × 20 / 56 × 60 ≈ 17 min. - Check against the real CTUN.ThH and BAT.Curr log after the first hover: a discrepancy 20% means an error in the weight or the table. Step 4. Overheating check The continuous motor current in hover should be well below the maximum in the table aim for ≤ 40% . Check after 5 minutes of hover: the motor is warm, not hot. Lab Do steps 1–3 for your own build with two prop options, pick one and justify it with numbers; after the flight, compare the calculated hover current with the log. diagnostics - Symptom: hover throttle above 60% - Possible cause: T/W too low: the prop is too small, the KV too low, or the mass has grown. - What to do: recalculate from the table, use a prop with a larger diameter/pitch, cut the mass. - Symptom: motors are hot after a short flight - Possible cause: the prop is too big or has too much pitch for the KV, so the current is above the continuous rating. - What to do: less pitch or diameter, check the hover current in the log. - Sympto

summary: The flight controller (FC) is a small computer that reads the sensors, runs the controller math and commands the motors thousands of times a second. text: summary The flight controller FC is a small computer that reads the sensors, runs the controller math and commands the motors thousands of times a second. This module explains what sits on the board, what each sensor is responsible for, how to read a wiring diagram and why the same wire behaves differently on different pads. After it, the board diagram stops being a puzzle. theory Processor The heart of the FC is a microcontroller. The series determines the capabilities: - F4 : the most common and cheapest; limited in the number of UARTs and can't invert UARTs in hardware see the SBUS module . - F7 : faster, more UARTs, software inversion. - H7 : the most powerful, the standard for ArduPilot and PX4 on complex platforms. What matters isn't “the best processor” but whether the firmware you need supports the board: each firmware has its own list of targets. Sensors - Gyroscope gyro : angular rate on three axes. The main sensor: stabilization runs on it. It's read thousands of times a second and is sensitive to vibration. - Accelerometer accel : acceleration; at rest it shows the direction of gravity. Needed for self-leveling modes ANGLE and navigation. - Barometer baro : pressure, and from it altitude. Sensitive to prop wash and to light, so it gets covered with foam. - Magnetometer mag, compass : heading. It's afraid of power wires: it goes on a mast together with the GPS, away from the current. - GPS : position and velocity. Needed for position hold, return to home and missions. Fusing these sensors is the job of the state estimation filter: in ArduPilot it's the EKF, in Betaflight a simplified scheme without navigation. Buses - UART : a serial port: receiver, GPS, VTX, telemetry, companion. Wires are crossed TX → RX . - I2C : a bus for several sensors compass, external baro, display over two wires, SDA/SCL. - SPI : a fast bus inside the board: gyro, OSD, flash for logs. Pads on the board Typical labels: VBAT battery voltage , 5V / 9V / 10V BEC outputs , GND , TX1 / RX1 UART1 , SDA / SCL I2C , CURR current sensor , LED addressable LEDs , BZ+ / BZ- buzzer , M1 – M4 or S1 – S8 outputs to ESCs/servos . Mounting The mounting standards are 30.5×30.5 and 20×20 mm. The board sits on rubber dampers: the gyro should feel the frame's motion, not its vibrations. The arrow on the board points “forward”; if the board is rotated, the rotation is set in the firmware board alignment / AHRS_ORIENTATION . A closer look at the gyro: chips and rates The gyro is a MEMS chip on SPI. Common ones: MPU6000 old, 8 kHz output, low noise, discontinued , ICM20602/20689 noisier, more sensitive to power , ICM42688-P the modern standard: up to 32 kHz, a configurable hardware anti-aliasing filter, low noise , BMI270 an alternative, 6.4 kHz . The firmware reads the chip over SPI at 8–24 MHz with DMA the “Embedded” module and runs the PID loop in sync with the gyro output always in 4.x; the PID loop divider is pid_process_denom : at 8 kHz that's every 125 µs. The chain: chip → hardware LPF gyro_hardware_lpf → software filters the “Filters” module → PID. Two gyros on a board dual gyro means averaging or selection; ArduPilot on H7 handles up to three IMUs with separate EKF cores. {{diagram:fc-signal-path The signal path inside the FC: gyro → filters → PID → mixer → ESC; the RC command sets the target, Blackbox and OSD take a copy.}} What else is on the board - OSD chip MAX7456 for analog or digital OSD via MSP DisplayPort DJI/Walksnail/HDZero : draws telemetry onto the video. - Flash/SD for Blackbox: 16–32 MB of flash is enough for minutes at 2 kHz; SD for hours. It's written over SPI/SDIO and sometimes conflicts over DMA with other functions on F4. - BEC : 5 V typically 2–3 A total for all loads and 9–12 V for the VTX/digital system, 2–3 A . The limits are in the board's description; don't power a Raspberry Pi from an FC pad the “Connecting peripherals” module . - Current sensor on the PDB/ESC → the CURR pad; the scale ibata_scale Betaflight / BATT_AMP_PERVLT ArduPilot is calibrated against a wattmeter. - UART inverters on F4 exist only on some ports for SBUS they're labeled “SBUS”/“RX” and have a hardware inverter ; F7/H7 invert any port in software. - Softserial : a UART emulated on GPIO: up to 19200 baud, loads the processor; for SmartAudio/telemetry, not for the receiver. What limits your choice of board The number of UARTs receiver + GPS + VTX + companion = 4 minimum , whether it has a baro and compass mandatory for INAV/ArduPilot , BEC current for the load, support for the target by the firmware you need and its version ArduPilot: hwdef , Betaflight: unified target , size and mass, 30.5/20 mm mounting, whether it has CAN DroneCAN on big aircraft , the number of motor/servo outputs VTOL needs 8+ . {{diagram:fc-board-choice-tree Выбор платы идёт от прошивки: навигации нужны баро, компас и не меньше 4 UART, а VTOL и большим аппаратам — H7 с CAN и 8+ выходами.}} Worked example: reading a pinout A typical H743 board 30.5 mm : UART1 is RX with an inverter labeled SBUS , UART2 is GPS with SDA/SCL next to it for the compass , UART4 is VTX/DisplayPort the 9V pad is next to it , UART6 / UART7 are companion/telemetry, M1–M8 are DShot, CURR is the current sensor from the ESC, LED is the addressable strip, BZ- is the buzzer, VBAT is voltage measurement, 5V is for the receiver/GPS, 4V5 is powered from USB for setup without a battery . The reading rule: power first what comes from where, how much current , then the UARTs by function, then I2C, then the “special” pads. Put the “pad → function → device → current” table into the build passport. practice Lab: read your board's diagram 1. Find the wiring diagram of your FC from the manufacturer. 2. Write down which UART is free for the receiver, which for the GPS, which for the VTX. 3. Find which pad powers the VTX and camera and how much current that BEC supplies. 4. Note whether there's a pad with an inverter for SBUS on F4 and where to solder the LED and buzzer. 5. Save the result in

summary: Half of all “tuning problems” are mechanical: an unbalanced prop, a loose motor, a frame that rings at a frequency where the motor harmonics land. Filters and PIDs treat the symptoms; this module is about the causes. Where vibration comes from, what frame resonance is, how to balance props and motor
headings: Sources of vibration Frame resonance How vibration ruins a flight Mounting the flight controller Numbers Natural frequencies: a rough estimate FC damping: how to choose Worked example: a 7" with a 180 Hz peak Step 1. Inspection Step 2. Balancing Step 3. Measure, don't feel Step 4. Wires Lab
text: summary Half of all “tuning problems” are mechanical: an unbalanced prop, a loose motor, a frame that rings at a frequency where the motor harmonics land. Filters and PIDs treat the symptoms; this module is about the causes. Where vibration comes from, what frame resonance is, how to balance props and motors, how to mount the flight controller and route the wires, and how to measure the result with a spectrum instead of by feel. theory Sources of vibration - Prop imbalance — the blades don't have equal mass: the force is ~ m·r·ω², so it grows with the square of RPM. The main source at the rotation frequency 1st harmonic . - Motor imbalance — the bell, the magnets; same frequency. - Blade aerodynamics — thrust pulsations at “RPM × number of blades” 2nd, 3rd harmonics . - Play and flex — a bearing, an under-tightened motor, a flexible arm: they add broadband noise and can “ring” at their own frequency. - Prop wash and turbulence — low-frequency shaking at 20–70 Hz; that's aerodynamics, not mechanics. Frame resonance A frame has natural frequencies the arms, the FC mount, the standoffs . When a motor harmonic passes through a natural frequency, the amplitude grows several times over. In the spectrum this is a peak that does not move with RPM. Resonance is not removed by the RPM filter it tracks the motors ; it is caught by the dynamic notch or eliminated by changing the structure: a stiffer arm, different mass, a damper. How vibration ruins a flight - The gyro sees vibration as angular rate → the PID “corrects” motion that doesn't exist → hot motors, mushy response. - The accelerometer clips saturates → the ArduPilot EKF loses its altitude and position estimate VIBE , Clip . - The barometer “breathes” from the airflow. Mounting the flight controller The goal is to pass the frame's motion through but not the high-frequency vibration. The standard: soft rubber grommets or standoffs with dampers, wires without tension a tight harness is a rigid link that bypasses the dampers . A mount that is too soft has its own low-frequency resonances and adds gyro lag. Big aircraft use damping plates; 5" racers often use a hard mount and a clean filter tune. Numbers Motor 1st-harmonic frequency = RPM/60. At hover: 5" ~250–350 Hz, 7" ~120–200, 10" ~80–100, 15" ~50–70. Carbon arm resonances are usually 100–400 Hz, FC mounts 50–150 Hz. Natural frequencies: a rough estimate An arm as a cantilever beam: f₁ ≈ 0.56·√ E·I/ μ·L⁴ E — Young's modulus, I — second moment of area of the cross-section, μ — mass per meter, L — length . For an engineering estimate it's easier to measure: tapping the arm with the accelerometer/gyro being logged LOG_DISARMED / blackbox_mode = ALWAYS gives a decaying oscillation — the frequency of the peak in the spectrum is the resonance. Typical values: 5" carbon arm 4–5 mm — 300–500 Hz above the motor harmonics at hover, below them at full throttle ; 7" 5 mm — 150–250 Hz matches the 1st–2nd harmonics — the danger zone ; 10"+ tube arms 16–25 mm — 60–150 Hz. Stiffen the arm thicker, shorter, a tube instead of a plate → the frequency rises as √ stiffness/mass ; add mass at the tip a heavier motor → it drops. FC damping: how to choose A rubber grommet is a spring with a damper: the natural frequency of the “board on grommets” system is f₀ = 1/2π ·√ k/m . You want f₀ 3–5 times below the lowest motor harmonic but above the control bandwidth ≥ 50–80 Hz : for a 5" motors at 250+ Hz — f₀ ≈ 60–80 Hz; for an X8 motors at 55 Hz , dampers with f₀ of 15–20 Hz are already “soft” and add lag — there you work through balancing and notches, not softness. Sign of a mount that is too soft: a low-frequency peak at 20–40 Hz in the spectrum and a “mushy” feel. Wires and ribbon cables bypass the dampers if they are tight. {{diagram:chart-fc-damper-window Окно мягкого крепления f₀ в 3–5 раз ниже гармоники моторов, но не ниже 50–80 Гц есть только при гармониках от 150–240 Гц: у 5" 250 Гц это 50–83 Гц, у 7" из примера 125 Гц , 10" и X8 окна нет — там балансировка и notch.}} Worked example: a 7" with a 180 Hz peak Spectrogram: a horizontal line at 180 Hz regardless of throttle, 25 dB above the noise floor; the motor harmonic at hover is 125 Hz, the 2nd is 250 Hz when throttling up it passes through 180 Hz — the resonance “rings” . Tap test on the arm — 182 Hz: it's the arm. Options: a 6 mm arm instead of 5 f ↑ ~20% → 215 Hz, moves away from the 1st harmonic, but the 2nd still passes through — not a solution; a dynamic notch at 180 helps, but adds delay — a stopgap; the real fix — move the motor mounting point/shorten the arm f ↑ by 1.3–1.5× , or accept it and set a static notch gyro_notch1_hz = 180 , cutoff = 150 . Write it into the build sheet: “arm resonance 180 Hz, notch”. Without a spectrum all of this would have looked like “you need to lower D”. {{diagram:vibration-path The vibration path from motors and propellers through the frame and mount to the gyro and the control loop — and where to break it.}} practice Step 1. Inspection 1. Props: cracks, chips, the same model and pitch on all motors. 2. Motors: up-and-down play in the bell, bearing grit when you spin it by hand, screw tightness no longer than needed — a screw in the winding = a short circuit . 3. Frame: cracks around the holes, standoffs tight, no wires touching the props. Step 2. Balancing 1. Props — on a balancer: the heavy blade drops; sand material off the back side near the tip, or add a drop of lacquer/a piece of tape to the light one. 2. Motors — run them without props at low throttle and touch the standoff: you can feel the vibrating motor. More precisely — a log spectrum without props. Step 3. Measure, don't feel 1. A hover log before any changes, the gyro spectrum Blackbox Explorer / PID Toolbox / your own Python . 2. Find the peaks: they follow throttle → motors; they stay put → resonance. 3. After balancing/a damper — the same flight, the same spectrum, the difference in dB in the peak's band. Step 4. Wires Harnesses not tight, not touching

title: PID controller in Betaflight
summary: The PID controller is the core of stabilization in Betaflight. This article explains the physical meaning of the P, I, D coefficients, how they interact, how they affect the drone's behavior, and how to tune them using Blackbox. After studying it, you will be able to diagnose typical problems (oscil
headings: The formula as implemented in `flight/pid.c` Mechanisms you won't find in a PID textbook Worked example: where bounce-back comes from
text: summary The PID controller is the core of stabilization in Betaflight. This article explains the physical meaning of the P, I, D coefficients, how they interact, how they affect the drone's behavior, and how to tune them using Blackbox. After studying it, you will be able to diagnose typical problems oscillations, bounce-back, motor overheating and adjust parameters deliberately instead of guessing at random. theory The PID controller Proportional-Integral-Derivative gets the angular rate on the roll, pitch, yaw axes from the gyro and minimizes the error between the desired rate setpoint, from the sticks or navigation and the current rotation rate. The controller output PID sum is converted into motor signals by the mixer. P-term proportional reacts to the current error: the bigger the error, the stronger the correction. It defines the drone's basic stiffness. Drawback: it cannot fully eliminate steady-state error drift . Too high, and it causes fast oscillations 20–50 Hz . I-term integral accumulates error over time, eliminating a constant offset drift from wind, a shifted center of mass . It works slower than P. Too high, and it causes slow floaty oscillations 1–5 Hz and wind-up. The iterm_limit parameter in 2025.12 — iterm_windup limits the maximum I-term value. D-term derivative reacts to the rate of change of the error, acting as a damper. It suppresses oscillations caused by the P-term. It is critically sensitive to gyro noise. Without filtering it produces high-frequency noise that overheats the motors. The rule: D-term is tuned after P-term; raising P requires raising D. Betaflight 4.5+ specifics: - Feedforward — an independent control path that feeds a signal straight to the motors based on how fast the stick moves. It speeds up the response without raising the P-term. - TPA Throttle PID Attenuation — reduces the PID coefficients at high throttle. In BF 4.5+ the default is tpa_mode = D reduces only the D-term ; PD is also available. - RPM Filtering — uses data from the ESC to suppress noise from the propellers. It creates narrow filters at the motors' rotation frequency, letting you raise the D-term. The formula as implemented in flight/pid.c For each axis on every loop at the PID rate : error e = setpoint − gyro filtered ; - P = Kp·e; - I += Ki·e·dt, limited by iterm_limit anti-windup and by “relax” below ; - D = −Kd·d gyro_D /dt — the derivative of the gyro , not of the error stick movement doesn't kick D , after the D filters the “Filters” module , with a multiplier from the d_min logic; - FF = Kff·d setpoint /dt with averaging/smoothing feedforward_averaging , feedforward_smooth_factor , feedforward_jitter_factor , feedforward_boost — an addition from the second derivative, feedforward_max_rate_limit ; - sum → TPA → pidSum → mixer. The coefficients from the configurator “45” are multiplied by the scale factors in pid_init.c P ≈ 0.032, I ≈ 0.244, D ≈ 0.00053, FF ≈ 0.0138 — that's Betaflight's “dimensionlessness”; the physical meaning can be recovered only through the response the “Control theory” module . Mechanisms you won't find in a PID textbook - I-term relax iterm_relax = RP , iterm_relax_type = SETPOINT , iterm_relax_cutoff = 15 : during fast stick movements I accumulation is paused — otherwise after a flip I “carries” extra rotation one of the kinds of bounce-back . Lower cutoff → more aggressive relax. - I-term rotation iterm_rotation : when rotating in yaw, the accumulated roll/pitch I is rotated together with the frame. - Anti-gravity anti_gravity_gain , anti_gravity_p_gain , anti_gravity_cutoff_hz : temporarily raises I and P on sharp throttle changes — against the “nose dip” when you punch the throttle. - D_min / D_max 4.5: d_min_ — base, d_ — peak; 2025.12: d_ — base, d_max_ — peak; plus d_max_gain , d_max_advance : D is low in calm flight less noise/heat and rises on fast moves and propwash, based on gyro/setpoint. - TPA tpa_mode = D by default in 4.5, tpa_rate , tpa_breakpoint ; 4.5+ also has tpa_low_ for low throttle : reduces D or PD above a throttle point — at high throttle thrust is more linear and noise is higher. - Thrust linearization thrust_linear and throttle boost : compensation for the nonlinearity of thrust vs. throttle and a short-term boost of the throttle response. - Air mode : PID works even at zero throttle feature AIRMODE or the AIR MODE mode , with a minimum idle dshot_idle_value ; in 2025.12 — motor_idle — otherwise the aircraft is uncontrollable when descending with no throttle. Worked example: where bounce-back comes from Log: after a sharp roll stick stop the gyro overshoots to −18% of the maneuver amplitude. Check in order: 1 the D filters are not too low delay — dterm_lpf1_dyn_max_hz 150 → ok; 2 enough D? Damping slider 1.0 → 1.15 — bounce-back 18 → 11%, motors warm; 3 I-relax on iterm_relax = RP — yes; 4 mechanics — the spectrum is clean. Result: Damping 1.15, entry in the decision table. If the motors had been heating up, the path would be the opposite: filters/mechanics, not D. {{diagram:bf-pid-terms PID in Betaflight: P and I from the error, D from the gyro with d_min , FF from the setpoint derivative; it all adds up into pidSum.}} practice {{widget:pid-sim}} Preparation Hardware requirements: ESC with RPM Filtering support BLHeli_32 or Bluejay , F7/H7 flight controller, SD card for Blackbox at least 4 GB . Software requirements: Betaflight Configurator 10.10+, Blackbox Explorer. Setup before tuning 1. Enable RPM Filtering: in the Motors tab turn on Bidirectional DShot and set Motor poles the RPM filter enables itself ; rpm_filter_q = 500 is the default value CLI . 2. Set up Blackbox: choose a 2 kHz logging rate, enable logging of gyro_scaled, pid, setpoint, motor. 3. Set the baseline filtering parameters: text set gyro_lpf2_static_hz = 300 set gyro_lpf2_type = PT2 set dterm_lpf2_static_hz = 150 set dterm_lpf2_type = PT2 set dyn_notch_max_hz = 600 set dyn_notch_q = 250 save Step-by-step tuning 1. text: summary The tip of a 5-inch prop moves at about 300 km/h and carries enough energy to cut skin down to the bone; a shorted LiPo dumps hundreds of amps and burns with its own oxidizer: you can knock the flame down, but the burning restarts until the cells cool off. Most injuries in the hobby happen not in the air but on the bench: the drone armed with props on during setup. This module gives you the physics of the danger in numbers, the rules that are not up for discussion, the full list of Betaflight arming disable flags from the source code, with explanations and the ArduPilot equivalent, pre-flight and post-flight checklists, and what to do in a battery fire. theory Danger in numbers - Propeller. Tip speed = π · D · n. For a 5" D = 0.127 m in hover at 14,000 rpm 233 rev/s : 0.40 m × 233 ≈ 93 m/s — about 335 km/h; unloaded, up to 30,000 rpm — 200 m/s. The kinetic energy of a spinning 5" prop ~4 g is a few joules: enough for deep cuts; 7–10" — tens of joules, broken fingers; 15" on an X8 — injuries that end your hobby. - Motors on the bench. A motor test in the configurator without removing the props is a classic injury. The firmware warns you but won't stop you. - LiPo. Internal resistance is 1–3 mΩ per cell: a short circuit of a 6S pack means hundreds of amps, and the wire glows hot within a second. A cell punctured in a crash can catch fire minutes or hours after the impact. The burning is thermal runaway with oxygen released from the cathode: knock the flame down ABC extinguisher, sand , then cool with plenty of water , or carry it outside in a non-flammable container and let it burn out. A class D extinguisher is designed for metallic lithium — LiPo and Li-Ion don't contain any. A puffed pack is retired: discharge it to 0 in salt water several days and dispose of it. - Link loss. If failsafe hasn't been tested on this aircraft, it will do something nobody chose module “Failsafe” . - The first flight after any change — a swapped motor, prop direction, wrong mixer, untested filter: statistically the most dangerous flight. How the firmware protects against arming Betaflight master; 2025.12 has no AUTOPILOT_SW , 4.5 has no FLIP_SWITCH / ALT_HOLD_SW / POS_HOLD_SW / AUTOPILOT_SW , and ARM_SWITCH is called ARMSWITCH Arming is impossible while at least one disable flag is active. The list lives in src/main/fc/runtime_config.c ; the flags are shown by status in the CLI and in the OSD the “Warnings” element : {{diagram:arming-tree “Won't arm” troubleshooting tree: read the flag first, then check the specific cause.}} Flag What it means What to do --- --- --- NOGYRO gyro not detected check the board/target, don't fly FAILSAFE / BOXFAILSAFE failsafe active no RC / failsafe switch on restore the link, turn the switch off RXLOSS no receiver signal bind, RX power, port protocol NOT_DISARMED not disarmed after… disarm with the switch RUNAWAY runaway takeoff protection triggered disarm; check motor/prop direction CRASH crash detector disarm/reboot THROTTLE throttle not at minimum throttle stick down, check min_check ANGLE tilt greater than small_angle level it, or small_angle = 180 for Acro BOOTGRACE not enough time since power-on wait NOPREARM PREARM not enabled enable PREARM LOAD CPU overload lower the loop rate/disable features CALIB calibration in progress wait CLI , CMS , MSP , BST CLI / OSD menu open / configurator connected close it — and that's how it should be PARALYZE PARALYZE mode activated reboot GPS GPS Rescue requires a fix, there isn't one wait for a fix or disable the requirement RESCUE_SW GPS Rescue switch on at arming turn it off DSHOT_TELEM RPM filter enabled, but no eRPM from the ESC dshot_bidir , ESC firmware, wires REBOOT_REQD reboot required after setup reboot DSHOT_BBANG bitbang DShot error check resources/timers NO_ACC_CAL accelerometer not calibrated calibrate MOTOR_PROTO motor protocol not configured select DShot FLIP_SWITCH , ALT_HOLD_SW , POS_HOLD_SW , AUTOPILOT_SW mode switch on at arming turn it off ARM_SWITCH ARM switch was on when connected turn it off and on again These flags are a safety net, not a nuisance. The rule: fix the cause, don't disable the check. ArduPilot : ARMING_SKIPCHK 4.7+, a bitmask of skipped checks; before 4.7 — ARMING_CHECK , a bitmask of enabled ones: baro, compass, GPS, INS, parameters, RC, voltage, geofence… , and “PreArm: …” messages in the GCS follow the same logic; skipping checks is acceptable only on a test stand. Modes and devices for protection - PREARM — a second switch without which arming is impossible; mandatory on aircraft with 7"+ props. - Failsafe — what to do on link loss; tested on the ground without props before the first flight of every new build. - Beeper and GPS in the OSD — to find a crashed aircraft. - Runaway takeoff prevention Betaflight runaway_takeoff_prevention = ON — disarms if, after arming, the gyro shows growing rotation that doesn't respond to control inputs swapped motors/props . - Low-battery buzzer, timer — so you don't keep flying on a depleted battery. Site and people The safe zone radius around takeoff is at least 10–15 m for a 5", 30 m for heavy aircraft; nobody stands in the plane of the props during arming; take off away from yourself. Rules and zones — module “Rules”, team organization — “Field Operations”. practice Pre-flight checklist print it 1. Props: intact, tightened, direction matches the motor diagram, no foreign objects in the prop plane. 2. Battery: no puffing or damage, per-cell voltage normal 4.1–4.2 V/cell when full , secured with a strap, XT connector not melted. 3. RC and VTX antennas: in place, intact, not in the prop plane; VTX with antenna attached without one it will burn out . 4. Radio: correct model, charged, ARM/PREARM switches off, failsafe test done on this aircraft. 5. Video/OSD: voltage, LQ/RSSI, warnings — no flags. 6. Zone: people and animals outside the radius, takeoff away from yourself, obstacles accounted for, site rules. 7. After arming: 2–3 s of hover at 0.5–1 m — res

text: summary A UAV engineer is responsible not only for making the aircraft fly, but also for where and how it flies. Rules differ from country to country and change every year, so this module doesn't retell them. Instead it teaches you to find the current ones, understand the common logic risk categories, zones, altitudes, registration, insurance and keep operator documentation. This is not legal advice: the source of truth is your country's regulator. theory The common logic of regulation Most countries build their rules around risk : aircraft mass, proximity to people and infrastructure, altitude, visibility. Typical elements: - Registration of the operator and/or the aircraft above a certain mass. - Operation categories : from “open” small aircraft, in visual line of sight, away from people to “specific” and “certified” authorizations, risk assessment . - Altitude limit above ground often around 120 m / 400 ft in the open category . - Zones : airports, cities, infrastructure sites, borders, military sites — prohibited or requiring authorization. - Visual line of sight VLOS as the baseline requirement; flights beyond it BVLOS need separate authorizations. - Night flights, flights over people — separate conditions. - Liability insurance — mandatory or strongly recommended. What this means for an engineer - Test flights are flights too: same rules. - Autonomous missions and BVLOS are almost always a separate category. Plan them legally or in a simulator. - RC and video frequencies are regulated separately: VTX power and bands, and the allowed ELRS/900 MHz channels, depend on the country. - Responsibility lies with the operator and the owner. The flight log is your protection in case of an incident. Operator documentation The minimum professionals keep: - Operator log : date, location, aircraft, duration, purpose, incidents. - Aircraft log : configurations, repairs, replacements, motor/battery hours. - Build sheet from the “Foundation” capstone : mass, power system, frequencies. - Site risk assessment : people, obstacles, zones, weather, failure plan. How two “reference” systems work so you understand your own - EASA EU : three categories — Open up to 25 kg, VLOS, ≤ 120 m, subcategories A1/A2/A3 by proximity to people and aircraft class C0–C4 classes C5/C6 are for the STS standard scenarios in the Specific category ; operator registration from 250 g or if there is a camera; online exam A1/A3, an additional one for A2 , Specific SORA risk assessment, authorization from the national authority or STS standard scenarios; this is where BVLOS, heavy aircraft and flights over people end up , Certified like manned aviation . Homebuilt aircraft are Open only in A1 < 250 g or A3 away from people , otherwise Specific. - FAA USA : Part 107 for commercial flying exam, certificate, ≤ 400 ft, VLOS, Remote ID , Recreational TRUST test, registration from 250 g, 400 ft, Remote ID , authorization for flights in controlled airspace via LAANC; BVLOS — waiver. What both have in common: registration and identification Remote ID / C class , risk-based category, altitude ~120 m/400 ft, VLOS, zones, operator responsibility. Check your own country against the same structure: “which category, what registration threshold, what altitude, what identification, what about BVLOS”. {{diagram:easa-open-category-tree Самодельный аппарат без маркировки класса попадает в A1 только при массе < 250 г и скорости < 19 м/с, иначе — в A3 до 25 кг; BVLOS, полёты над скоплениями людей и аппараты от 25 кг — Specific.}} Radio frequencies: what is usually restricted The ISM bands 2.4 GHz, 5.8 GHz, 868/915 MHz are open for license-free use with a power limit in the EU 2.4 GHz — 100 mW EIRP, 5.8 GHz video — 25 mW EIRP under the general rules; 868 MHz — 25 mW with a duty cycle limit; in the USA it's different, 900 MHz is wider — a 1 W VTX or ELRS is formally outside the general rules in most countries and requires an amateur radio license or a separate authorization. The course modules on link budget compute the physics; whether the power is legal is a separate question you settle before the flight. Worked example: test flights of a homebuilt 7" A 1.4 kg aircraft, homebuilt no C class , with a camera. EU: Open A3 — ≥ 150 m from residential/industrial/recreational areas, away from people, ≤ 120 m, operator registration, A1/A3 exam, insurance as your country requires; any BVLOS test or autonomous mission test beyond VLOS is Specific. USA: recreational TRUST, registration, Remote ID module or Part 107, 400 ft, LAANC if needed. The takeaway for your engineering folder: site, category, documents, what is not allowed — written down before the first flight; autonomous tests go to SITL and a tethered test stand until you have an authorization. {{diagram:airspace-check Pre-flight check logic: zone status on the official map, category rules and allowed radio frequencies specific values follow your country's legislation .}} practice Step 1. Find your country's rules 1. Your country's civil aviation regulator — the official website, the section on drones. 2. Write down with links: registration from what mass , categories, altitude, zones, VLOS/BVLOS, insurance. 3. Separately — the radio frequency rules VTX power, bands . 4. The date you checked goes in the note: check again in a year. Step 2. Zone map around your site Find the official zone map many regulators have a service or an app . Mark the nearest airports and restricted zones, figure out where you can fly without an authorization. Step 3. Start the logs Two files in your drone repository: operator-log.md and <drone /log.md . The first entry is today. Step 4. Site risk assessment A one-page checklist: people and animals, obstacles and wires, zone and altitude, weather wind, precipitation, battery temperature , plan for link loss where it falls on DROP, where it flies on RTH , emergency services contact. Rules summary template Item What the rule says Link document, clause Date checked --- --- --- ---

text: summary Eighty percent of real engineering work isn't tuning, it's choosing: what to buy so the drone does the job, stays within budget and doesn't fall apart. This module gives you a method: the mission in numbers → aircraft class → frame and props → motors and ESC → battery → FC and peripherals → mass and T/W check → two alternatives. With a T/W and flight time calculator and a walkthrough of two specifications: a 7" long-range and a 10" heavy-lift. theory Step 0: the mission in numbers As long as the mission sounds like “I want to fly far,” there's nothing to choose. You need numbers: Parameter Example: 7" long-range Example: 10" heavy-lift --- --- --- Payload 30 g camera 1000 g load Flight time ≥ 15 min ≥ 12 min with the load Range 5 km 1 km Cruise speed 15–20 m/s 8 m/s Conditions wind up to 8 m/s wind up to 6 m/s Budget €400 €700 Constraints mass < 1 kg category foldable Each number becomes a requirement with an ID in the engineering folder next module . Step 1: class and frame Prop size determines everything else. The rule: payload mass and flight time set the required efficiency g/W , and efficiency sets the prop diameter see the aerodynamics module : 5" gives 4–6 g/W, 7" gives 8–10, 10" gives 12–15, 15" gives 15–20. Long hover with a load means big props; speed and maneuverability mean small ones. Frame: 3–5 mm carbon arms for 5–7", 5–6 mm or tubes for 10"+. Look at: mass, free space for the battery and payload, protection of the electronics, availability of spare parts you should be able to buy an arm separately , a 20×20 or 30.5×30.5 mm stack. Step 2: motors and props From the manufacturer's thrust table for the chosen prop and voltage: hover thrust should fall at 30–45% throttle headroom for wind and maneuvers at a current no higher than 40% of the continuous rating. Motor size and KV: 7" uses 2806.5/2807 1300–1700 KV on 6S; 10" uses 3110/3115 600–900 KV on 6S; 15" uses 4008–4114 320–400 KV on 6S. Motor mass goes into the mass budget. {{diagram:component-choice-tree Power system guidelines for typical aircraft classes.}} Step 3: ESC ESC continuous current ≥ 1.3 × the motor's maximum current from the table; voltage with margin 6S → an ESC rated for 6S, not one that's “up to 6S” at its limit . A 4-in-1 is compact, but one crash means replacing the whole thing; separate ESCs are repairable, but you have to route power to each. The firmware BLHeli_32/AM32/BLHeli_S determines telemetry and the RPM filter. Step 4: battery Capacity from current: I_avg from the table for cruise/hover × number of motors + electronics × t / 0.8. Chemistry: LiPo for current, Li-Ion for energy per kilogram but its discharge capability is low: typically 2–3C for high-capacity 21700 cells . Check: does the battery mass fit the mass budget? If not, iterate: heavier battery → more current → an even bigger battery. This loop doesn't always converge; if it doesn't, change the class. Step 5: FC, receiver, video, GPS FC: an F4 is enough for Betaflight without extras, an F7/H7 for INAV/ArduPilot with GPS, compass and logs; number of UARTs ≥ number of peripherals + 1; a blackbox flash/SD for log-based tuning. Receiver: a band to match the range 900 MHz for 5+ km . Video: analog is cheap and tough, digital means quality and budget. GPS: with a compass on a mast for INAV/ArduPilot. Step 6: mass budget and check A table: part, mass, price. The result: takeoff mass → T/W from the motor table → hover current → flight time → comparison with the requirements. The rule: if T/W < 2 at full load, redo it. Keep a 15% margin in the budget for props, hardware, wires and repairs. Trade-offs - Price vs mass : cheap components are heavier; mass means flight time and current. - Repairability : a drone built from small, available parts lives longer than an exotic one. - Margin : 20% of headroom in current and thrust pays for itself on the first windy day. - Availability : a part that's out of stock six months from now is a problem at the first repair. The calculator below computes T/W, hover current and flight time from your numbers; use it in step 6. practice {{widget:tw-calc}} Step 1. Requirements A table of the mission in numbers for your own drone idea as in the theory , 8–12 rows. Step 2. Specification A component table: model, mass, price, a link to the data source thrust table, datasheet . Totals for mass and price. Step 3. Calculation With the calculator: T/W, hover throttle, current, flight time. Compare with the requirements and write down which ones are met. Step 4. Alternatives Two options for example, 7" Li-Ion vs 7" LiPo; or a 10" quad vs a 7" with a smaller load in one table by criteria: time, price, mass, repairability, risk. Justify the choice. Worked calculation The calculator's default values: mass 1400 g, 4 motors with 1200 g maximum thrust each, 6.5 g/W in hover, 6S 4000 mAh, electronics 0.8 A. - T/W = 4 · 1200 / 1400 = 3.43, hover throttle ≈ 1 / 3.43 ≈ 29% — in the linear "thrust ∝ throttle" approximation; thrust grows faster than throttle T ∝ n² , so the real hover throttle is higher: with a MOT_THST_EXPO = 0.65 curve, about 45%. - Motor power in hover: 1400 g / 6.5 g/W ≈ 215 W; current 215 / 6 · 3.7 + 0.8 ≈ 10.5 A. - Hover on 80% of capacity: 4 · 0.8 / 10.5 · 60 ≈ 18 minutes. In flight with maneuvers and wind, 20–40% less. - Add 400 g of load 1800 g : T/W 2.67, throttle 38%, current 13.3 A, hover ≈ 14.5 minutes. That's the price of every gram in minutes of flight. What to write down and how to check yourself - Requirements table: every row has a number and a unit. “Flies for a long time” isn't a requirement; “≥ 15 minutes of hover with a 300 g load” is. - Specification: every component has a source for its numbers: the manufacturer's thrust table, a datasheet, weighing. A mass without wires, connectors and hardware is 5–10% too low; add that as a separate row. - Calculation: mark which requirements are met, which aren't, and by how much. text: summary Первый комплект — это пять покупок, которые зависят друг от друга: пульт, видеосистема с очками, аппарат, питание и инструмент. Ошибка в порядке стоит дороже ошибки в модели: очки не той системы превращают следующий аппарат в несовместимый, а приёмник не той версии ELRS не свяжется с пультом. Модуль даёт порядок решений, таблицы классов с диапазонами цен на ноябрь 2026 года, матрицу совместимости очков DJI, список «не покупай первым» и чек-лист б/у. В лабораторной ты собираешь комплект под заданный бюджет и задачу, проверяешь совместимость по таблице и считаешь итог, массу и минуты в воздухе. theory Порядок решений: что переживает что Покупай от долгоживущего к расходному: 1. Пульт — служит дольше всего: он не падает и подходит к любому аппарату с тем же радиопротоколом. 2. Симулятор — пульт подключается к ПК по USB как джойстик. Oscar Liang руководство обновлено в ноябре 2026 советует минимум 5–10 часов до первого реального полёта. Выбор симулятора и программа тренировок с критериями — в ops-pilot-training . 3. Видеосистема и очки — выбор системы запирает тебя в экосистеме: видеопередатчик каждого следующего аппарата обязан подходить к этим очкам. 4. Аппарат — расходник. Первый ты разобьёшь, это норма. 5. АКБ, зарядка, инструмент — подбираются под класс аппарата число банок, разъём . {{diagram:starter-kit-order Сначала покупают то, что живёт дольше: пульт и очки остаются на годы, аппарат и АКБ меняются. Очки выбирают раньше аппарата, потому что видеопередатчик обязан совпасть с системой очков.}} Ориентир по сумме оценка Oscar Liang, ноябрь 2026 : аппарат 100–500 $, пульт 50–300 $, очки 50–900 $, АКБ 20–100 $, зарядка 30–200 $ — всего примерно 250–2000 $. Геймпад или клавиатура вместо пульта? Симулятор их примет, но ход стиков и центрирование другие, а пульт всё равно придётся купить. Учись сразу на нём. Пульт: классы и на что смотреть Минимальные требования: прошивка EdgeTX , встроенный модуль ExpressLRS 2.4 ГГц , гимбалы на датчиках Холла, USB-C с режимом джойстика. Текущая стабильная EdgeTX — 2.12.5 17 октября 2026 . Пульты на STM32F2 остались на ветке 2.11 2.11.8, только исправления — это важно для б/у. Цены — сайт RadioMaster и статьи Oscar Liang, ноябрь 2026, оценки без доставки и налогов. Устроен он не так, как 5": одна плата «5-в-1» вместо стека, приёмник ELRS внутри прошивки полётника, а половину потерь напряжения даёт разъём и сама банка. После модуля
