title: Digital FPV video: DJI, Walksnail, HDZero, OpenIPC
summary: The analog VTX from the “VTX Tables” module means minimal latency and graceful degradation into noise. Digital systems give you a picture that's many times sharper, onboard HD recording and a high-resolution OSD, but they pay for it with compression, latency that depends on the mode, and the “cliff”
headings: What changes when you go digital Four families HD OSD: MSP DisplayPort Frequencies and neighbors How to choose Step 1. Inventory your system Step 2. HD OSD Step 3. Latency Step 4. Edge of range on the ground
text: summary The analog VTX from the “VTX Tables” module means minimal latency and graceful degradation into noise. Digital systems give you a picture that's many times sharper, onboard HD recording and a high-resolution OSD, but they pay for it with compression, latency that depends on the mode, and the “cliff”: a freeze instead of snow. This module explains how analog, frame-synchronous digital HDZero , compressed video DJI, Walksnail and the open OpenIPC + WFB-ng combo fundamentally differ; how to hook up HD OSD via MSP DisplayPort in Betaflight, INAV and ArduPilot; and how to pick a system for the task rather than by the marketing. The lab is measuring the latency and the behavior at the edge of range of your own system. theory What changes when you go digital - Compression. Camera → H.264/H.265 encoder → radio → decoder → screen. The encoder looks for similarities between frames; the lower the bitrate, the more it has to “make things up”. Hence the artifacts on fast passes over grass and trees — where frames are least alike. - Latency is not one number. Manufacturers quote the minimum in the best mode high frame rate, strong signal . At the edge of range, systems lower the bitrate and frame rate, and latency grows. Compare systems by measuring in your own modes, not by the box. - Degradation. Analog at the edge means noise and stripes, but there's still a picture, and the pilot sees where they're flying. Digital holds a clean picture almost to the end, then freezes or breaks up into blocks. Behavior at link loss is the main safety question for long-range flights: what the pilot will see one second before losing video, and what the aircraft will do. - Onboard recording. Digital air units record video without radio losses — that's the “HD DVR” for flight review, as opposed to recording in the goggles. Four families System Principle Strength Limitations --- --- --- --- Analog 5.8 GHz uncompressed composite signal minimal and constant latency, graceful degradation, cheap low sharpness, interference shows immediately HDZero digital without inter-frame compression, synchronous with the camera frame low and stable latency, predictable for racing less sharp than compressed systems, blocks at the edge DJI O3/O4 , Walksnail Avatar compressed H.264/H.265 video with bitrate adaptation best picture, onboard recording, good range latency depends on the mode, closed ecosystem, fewer simultaneous channels OpenIPC + WFB-ng open IP camera firmware + Wi-Fi adapters in monitor mode, FEC openness, tunable for the task, MAVLink telemetry in the same channel built and configured by hand, higher latency than FPV systems Latency, resolution and range figures for specific models change with every generation and firmware — check the manufacturer's documentation for your version and, most importantly, measure. HD OSD: MSP DisplayPort In digital systems the OSD is drawn by the goggles or the air unit, and the flight controller only sends what to draw, using the MSP DisplayPort protocol over UART. - Betaflight 4.4+ : a UART on the Ports tab — MSP function for the air unit Peripherals: VTX MSP + DisplayPort ; in the CLI set osd_displayport_device = MSP , video system set vcd_video_system = HD . OSD elements are laid out on a larger canvas. - INAV : a UART with MSP DisplayPort for HD OSD, OSD type per your system's documentation. - ArduPilot : SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 42 DisplayPort , OSD_TYPE = 5 MSP DisplayPort . - VTX control channel, power on digital systems goes either through the same MSP or from the goggles menu — analog VTX tables aren't needed here. Frequencies and neighbors Digital systems also work in 5.8 GHz and occupy a wider band, so fewer of them fit in the air at the same time than analog aircraft on Raceband. At a shared field, agree on channels in advance; mixed analog + digital is a common source of mutual interference. Power and permitted channels — per your country's rules. How to choose - Racing and practicing in a crowd : analog or HDZero — constant low latency, lots of channels. - Freestyle and filming : DJI or Walksnail — the picture and recording matter more than a few milliseconds. - Long-range autopilot flights : what matters more is behavior at the edge and the telemetry link; digital video + a separate RC link ELRS + an OSD with the key data; OpenIPC — if you need an open system and MAVLink in the video channel. - An aircraft with a companion computer and vision : video for the pilot and video for the algorithm are different streams; don't tie navigation to the pilot's video channel. {{diagram:fpv-video-choice Choosing an FPV video system by task: constant low latency — analog or HDZero, picture and recording — DJI/Walksnail, openness and MAVLink in the channel — OpenIPC.}} practice Step 1. Inventory your system Air unit and goggles model, firmware version, modes resolution, frame rate, bitrate , antennas and their polarization, channel. Write it into the aircraft's logbook. Step 2. HD OSD Connect the air unit to a flight controller UART, set up MSP DisplayPort Betaflight: osd_displayport_device = MSP , vcd_video_system = HD ; ArduPilot: SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 42 , OSD_TYPE = 5 . Display voltage, current, RSSI/LQ, flight time, warnings. Check that the elements don't cover the center of the frame. Step 3. Latency The method from the “Cameras and Video Stream” module: a stopwatch with milliseconds on a phone screen, the aircraft camera looks at it, and the goggles or their output/recording are filmed by a second phone together with the original screen. 10 measurements in each mode for example, 60 and 100 fps, or two bitrate modes , median and maximum. Write down a table. Step 4. Edge of range on the ground Aircraft on a tripod, the pilot walks away or blocks the line of sight a building corner, trees — at reduced power so you don't have to walk far. Write down: at what RSSI/link quality the bitrate drops, latency grows, blocks appear, freeze. For analog if you have it — the same for comparison. Conclu

text: summary Обзор четырёх семейств цифрового видео — в link-digital-video , VTX-таблицы аналога — в link-vtx . Здесь — как подключить конкретный воздушный модуль к полётнику Betaflight 2025.12, чтобы он не сгорел, OSD появился в очках, а запись и мощность были настроены. Для DJI O3, O4, старые Air Unit и Vista , Walksnail Avatar и HDZero: питание, разводка, маска порта, osd_displayport_device , vcd_video_system , канва, шрифты, сторона очков, порядок включения, нагрев, запись, мощность, задержка и аналоги в INAV и ArduPilot. Лабораторная — Python-калькулятор по логике прошивки маски портов, проверка isSerialConfigValid , перенос элементов OSD между канвами по osd.h , затем стол: прозвонка, вентилятор, линк, OSD, запись. theory Кто что делает В цифровой системе OSD рисуют очки. Полётник только сообщает, какой символ и в какой клетке сетки нарисовать: команды MSP DisplayPort MSP_DP_WRITE_STRING , MSP_DP_DRAW_SCREEN , heartbeat идут по одному UART. По тому же UART воздушный модуль может управлять VTX по MSP канал, мощность, pit mode и сообщает полётнику размер своей сетки — канвы. Поэтому для HD-видео нужны три вещи: правильная разводка UART, правильная маска функций порта и HD-режим OSD. Если не хватает хотя бы одной, получается главный вопрос форумов: видео есть, OSD нет. Три системы: питание и провода Цифры взяты из документации производителей ссылки в references . Питание — главное, что отличает модели внутри одной системы. Система / модель Питание по спецификации Откуда брать UART провод модуля → пад FC RC из очков Задержка заявлено --- --- --- --- --- --- DJI FPV Air Unit 2019 7.4–17.6 В, 4–9 Вт VBAT 2S–4S MSP по UART DJI-пульт → S.Bus < 28 мс 720p/120 Caddx Vista 7.4–26.4 В VBAT 2S–6S как у Air Unit то же 21–28 мс 720p/120 DJI O3 Air Unit 7.4–26.4 В 2S–6S VBAT или BEC белый UART_RX → TX, серый UART_TX → RX, чёрный и коричневый — земли жёлтый DJI HDL/S.Bus → S.Bus-пад < 28 мс 810p/120 Goggles V2 , 30 мс 1080p/100 Goggles 2 DJI O4 Air Unit 3.7–13.2 В, BEC ≥ 10 Вт только BEC 5 В/2 А те же цвета то же от 20 мс 1080p/100 Goggles 3 DJI O4 Air Unit Pro 7.4–26.4 В, BEC ≥ 13.5 Вт VBAT или BEC 9 В/1.5 А те же цвета то же от 15 мс 1080p/100 Goggles 3 Walksnail Avatar HD Pro 6–25.2 В VBAT 6S — с конденсатором 50 В/47 мкФ RX модуля → TX, TX модуля → RX нет, отдельный приёмник в среднем 22 мс Walksnail Avatar Mini V3 3.1–13 В 1–3S 4S и выше — только через BEC то же нет в среднем 22 мс HDZero Race V3 4–12 В, 5–6 Вт BEC 5–12 В белый TX → RX, жёлтый RX → TX нет модель: ≈ 3 мс + период кадра 14 мс при 90 к/с HDZero Freestyle V2 7–25 В, 6–15 Вт BEC рекомендуется жёлтый RX → TX, белый TX → RX нет то же Правила, которые следуют из таблицы: - Модуль с верхним пределом 13 В от 4S напрямую не питать: у заряженного 3S LiHV 13.05 В, у 4S 16.8 В. HDZero прямо пишет, что, кроме Freestyle второй партии и новее, их VTX не рассчитаны на 6S VBAT, и рекомендует BEC: он гасит выбросы напряжения, которые убивают VTX. Площадка «10V/12V HD» на полётнике обычно подходит для любого модуля из таблицы, но её ток надо сверить с 13.5 Вт O4 Pro и 15 Вт Freestyle V2. Расчёт ветки — в el-power-design . - TX↔RX всегда крест-накрест, логика 3.3 В. У DJI два провода земли: силовая и сигнальная. Обе идут на полётник. - Управление с очков есть только у DJI. Жёлтый провод S.Bus подключается на S.Bus-пад полётника, serialrx_provider = SBUS , на F4 — пад с инвертором bf-ports . Если управление идёт по ELRS, жёлтый провод не подключают, а приёмник ставят на свой UART с CRSF. - SoftSerial для DisplayPort не годится: HDZero это прямо запрещает, а Betaflight вырезает MSP с SoftSerial-портов при проверке конфига см. ниже . {{diagram:bf-hd-wiring Разобранный пример: ELRS на UART1, воздушный модуль на UART4 с маской 131073 = MSP + VTX_MSP; питание модуля по его спецификации — от VBAT или только от BEC.}} Сторона Betaflight: маска порта Вкладка Ports хранит для каждого порта строку serial <id <маска <msp_baud <gps_baud <telemetry_baud <blackbox_baud id : 0 = UART1 … 9 = UART10, 20 = USB VCP, 30/31 = SoftSerial, 40 = LPUART1 . Маска — сумма битов serialPortFunction_e из io/serial.h . Для видео важны четыре бита: MSP = 1, VTX SmartAudio = 2048, VTX Tramp = 8192, VTX_MSP = 131072 1 << 17 . Пункт Peripherals «VTX MSP + DisplayPort » вместе с включённым MSP даёт маску 131073 . Значение 131072 из аудита курса по исходнику 4.5 и 2025.12 подтверждено, но это один бит VTX_MSP. На порту должно стоять 131073. Что прошивка делает с маской при загрузке io/serial.c , config/config.c ; логика одинакова в 4.5 и 2025.12 : 1. isSerialConfigValid : VTX_MSP в одиночку недопустим, только вместе с MSP или Serial RX. MSP может быть не больше чем на 3 портах, на VCP MSP обязателен. MSP и Serial RX на SoftSerial молча снимаются. При любом нарушении весь конфиг портов сбрасывается к умолчаниям платы, и приёмник «пропадает» вместе с OSD. 2. Порт для DisplayPort ищется так: первый порт, кроме VCP, у которого одновременно стоят MSP и VTX_MSP. Отдельной переменной для выбора порта больше нет. displayport_msp_serial существовала в 4.2–4.3 и удалена в 4.4 в settings.c веток 4.4, 4.5 и 2025.12 её нет . Аудит называл её параметром 4.4 — это неточность. Инструкции DJI O3/O4 и старая quickstart Walksnail до сих пор её показывают с оговоркой «для 4.3». И на 4.5, и на 2025.12 команда set displayport_msp_serial вернёт ошибку INVALID NAME . 3. Скорость — поле msp_baud , 115200. HDZero поддерживает 115200 и 230400 Race V3 — только 115200 , DJI и Walksnail в инструкциях указывают 115200. Режим HD и канва - vcd_video_system = HD . При HD fc/init.c берёт MSP-дисплей независимо от osd_displayport_device . Сам OSD должен быть включён feature OSD , тумблер OSD в Configuration . - osd_displayport_device = MSP варианты NONE , AUTO , MAX7456 , MSP , FRSKYOSD . - Умолчания зависят от опций Cloud Build. Если в сборке есть «OSD HD » USE_OSD_HD , то vcd_video_system = HD , osd_displayport_device = MSP , канва 53×20 OSD_HD_COLS/ROWS в osd.h . Только «OSD SD » — AUTO и 30×16. В сборке без HD-опции включ

text: summary The RC link controls the vehicle, while telemetry connects it to the ground station: map, mission, parameters, warnings. On a 5" ELRS telemetry is enough; a vehicle flying a mission several kilometers out needs a MAVLink channel with known range, throughput and diagnostics. This module covers the SiK family 433/868/915 MHz, 100 mW and RFD900 up to 1 W , setting them up with AT commands and what each parameter means, RADIO_STATUS and fade margin, ELRS in MAVLink mode, IP radios and mesh for multiple vehicles and video, LTE for beyond-the-horizon flights — and how to pick a channel for the job. theory What you need from telemetry - Throughput. A typical set of ArduPilot MAVLink streams is a few kilobytes per second; parameter and mission uploads are bursts. 64 kbit/s over the air ≈ 8 KB/s is plenty, 2–8 kbit/s is enough only for a minimal set of messages. - Range is set by the link budget the “Radio Link Budget” module : power, antennas, frequency, receiver sensitivity. Sensitivity improves as you lower the air data rate — roughly 3 dB for every halving; 6 dB of margin means twice the range. - Latency and duplex. SiK is time-division TDM : the transmitters take turns, latency is tens of milliseconds. For real-time control a joystick over telemetry this matters, for missions it doesn't. - Legality. 433, 868 and 915 MHz have different power and duty-cycle rules in different regions; you configure the modem for your country MIN_FREQ , MAX_FREQ , TXPOWER , DUTY_CYCLE . SiK: the parameters you need to understand SiK firmware runs on most “3DR/Holybro telemetry radios” and on the RFD900x its own branch . Set it up in Mission Planner SiK Radio or by hand: +++ with a one-second pause before and after → OK , ATI5 — list the parameters, ATSn=x — write one, AT&W — save, ATZ — reboot; RT instead of AT does the same for the remote modem. Register Parameter Meaning --- --- --- S1 SERIAL_SPEED UART baud rate in “one-byte form” 57 = 57600 ; the same on the flight controller S2 AIR_SPEED air data rate, kbit/s; 64 by default, lower means farther but slower S3 NETID network ID, identical within a pair; different for neighboring vehicles S4 TXPOWER power, dBm 20 = 100 mW on SiK; up to 30 = 1 W on RFD900x S5 ECC error-correcting code: halves the useful data rate, not recommended S6 MAVLINK 1 — aligns to MAVLink packets and injects RADIO_STATUS ; 2 — also prioritizes RC_OVERRIDE S8/S9 MIN_FREQ / MAX_FREQ frequency range, kHz — per your country's rules S10 NUM_CHANNELS number of frequency-hopping FHSS channels S11 DUTY_CYCLE share of time spent transmitting, %; 100 if the rules don't limit it S15 MAX_WINDOW TDM window, ms; smaller means lower latency and lower throughput Both sides must match in AIR_SPEED , NETID , ECC , MIN/MAX_FREQ , NUM_CHANNELS , otherwise the modems won't link. {{diagram:chart-sik-airspeed Relative SiK range versus air data rate: going from 64 down to 16 kbit/s gains about 6 dB and roughly twice the range.}} RADIO_STATUS and fade margin With MAVLINK = 1 the modem injects the RADIO_STATUS message id 109 into the stream: rssi , remrssi signal at the local and remote end , noise , remnoise , txbuf free space in the transmit buffer, % , error counters. ArduPilot uses txbuf to lower stream rates on its own when the link can't keep up — which is why SERIAL_SPEED can be higher than what the air link carries. - Converting RSSI to dBm approximately : dBm ≈ RSSI / 1.9 − 127. - Fade margin ≈ RSSI − noise / 2, dB. Every 6 dB of margin is a twofold range reserve: 18 dB at the test distance ≈ ×8. - 1 m test: RSSI on both sides above ~190 on a standard SiK; lower means a damaged antenna or modem. Other options - RFD900x/ux — the same SiK logic, 900 MHz, up to 1 W, diversity antennas; for long-range planes and VTOL. More power also means tougher requirements on the power supply pulse current and on antenna separation from the GNSS. - ELRS in MAVLink mode ELRS 3.5+ — RC and MAVLink telemetry over one link; telemetry reaches the GCS through the TX Backpack over Wi-Fi UDP 14550 or over the transmitter's own USB 460800 . Pro: one radio channel and ELRS range; con: a narrow telemetry pipe, so streams get trimmed. In ArduPilot, the receiver port: SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 , SERIALn_BAUD = 460 , RSSI_TYPE = 5 , stream rates for that port — 1 Hz; receiver and transmitter on ELRS 3.5.0+, TX Backpack 1.5.0+ details on the MAVLink page of the ELRS documentation . - Herelink and similar “all-in-one” systems — RC, HD video and telemetry in one radio with an Android GCS. - IP radios and mesh Microhard, Doodle Labs, Silvus and others — an Ethernet bridge over radio: MAVLink over UDP, video, SSH to the companion, several vehicles on one network. Expensive, but the standard for serious systems; routing is covered in the mav-routing module. - LoRa — very long range at a few kbit/s: fine for a minimal set position, status , not for parameters and missions. - LTE/4G — beyond-the-horizon link through a carrier network the “Cellular Bridge” project : range is limited by coverage, latency is 50–200 ms with unpredictable dropouts; you need a VPN or a relay because of NAT, and a mandatory link-loss failsafe. {{diagram:chart-elrs-param-download Время загрузки пропорционально числу параметров на логарифмических осях — параллельные прямые : 1000 параметров — 15.6 с на F1000 и 336 с на 50Hz, поэтому параметры грузят на быстром режиме на земле.}} How to choose Task Channel --- --- Missions within 1–3 km, simple GCS SiK 100 mW, AIR_SPEED 64 Long-range plane, 10+ km RFD900x, directional antenna on the ground, lower AIR_SPEED FPV/small vehicle, a single radio channel ELRS in MAVLink mode Video + telemetry + several vehicles IP radio / mesh Beyond the horizon, within coverage LTE + VPN, backup radio channel Redundancy: two independent telemetry channels e.g. SiK + LTE on different flight controller ports — the GCS sees the vehicle through either one. practice Step 1. Wind profile Step 2. Your aircraft's limit Step 3. Density altitude Step 4. Decoding a report Step 5. Your own “go / no-go” sheet
text: summary Half of all “unexplained” aircraft losses are weather nobody did the math on: the wind at 100 m is twice as strong as at the ground, heat in the mountains ate the thrust margin, a cold battery sagged on takeoff, fog coated the propellers with ice. This module gives you the calculations you do before you leave for the field: the wind profile with height and gusts, the wind limit for your own aircraft, density altitude and what it does to thrust and flight time, batteries in the cold, icing conditions, reading METAR/TAF aviation reports — and pulls them together into a “go / no-go” sheet with numbers. theory Wind: one thing at the ground, another at height - Profile. Friction with the ground slows the air down: wind increases with height. A simple model is the power law v h = v₁₀· h/10 ^α, where v₁₀ is the wind at 10 m that's where weather stations measure it , α ≈ 1/7 for open terrain, more 0.2–0.3 over forest and buildings. Example: 7 m/s at 10 m → at 100 m 7·10^ 1/7 ≈ 9.7 m/s. - Gusts. The mean wind is not the maximum. Reports give gusts separately G in METAR ; if they are missing, assume a factor of 1.3–1.5 over the mean. - Mechanical turbulence. Behind buildings, tree lines or a hill there are eddies extending downwind for several obstacle heights. Takeoff and landing on the downwind side of an obstacle is the bumpiest place. - Thermals. During the day, rising air over heated ground; for light aircraft and mapping, morning and evening are better. The wind limit for your aircraft - Multicopter. Flying into the wind, the aircraft is tilted; the stronger the wind, the more tilt and throttle. A practical rule: gusts no more than ~50–60 % of the aircraft's maximum horizontal speed in a position-hold mode — the rest is margin for maneuvering and returning. Check it in the log: average tilt and throttle while hovering in the wind; a hover throttle above ~70 % means there is no margin. - Plane. The wind must be noticeably below cruise speed: with a 15 m/s wind and an 18 m/s cruise, the ground speed into the wind is 3 m/s, and the return takes six times longer. - Route planning. Fly out into the wind, come back downwind: on the way back, when the battery is weaker, the wind helps. If the route is the reverse, calculate the return time using the ground speed into the wind. {{diagram:chart-wind-profile Wind versus height for 10 m/s at 10 m: at 100 m the mean is ~14 m/s, gusts ×1.4 — about 20 m/s.}} Density altitude Propeller thrust is proportional to air density ρ, and the power needed to hover at the same thrust is proportional to 1/√ρ from momentum theory, module “Propeller aerodynamics” . Density drops with altitude and with temperature. - Density altitude is the altitude in the standard atmosphere ISA: 15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level, −6.5 °C per km at which the density is the same as it is now. Estimate: density altitude ≈ pressure altitude + ~36 m for every °C above the ISA temperature at that altitude. - Example. A site at 2000 m, +30 °C. The ISA temperature at 2000 m is +2 °C, the deviation is +28 °C → density altitude ≈ 2000 + 28·36 ≈ 3000 m. Density is ~74 % of sea level: maximum thrust drops to ~74 %, hover power rises by ~16 %, flight time drops by roughly the same amount, and a 2:1 thrust-to-weight ratio turns into ~1.5:1. - What to do. Recalculate thrust-to-weight and flight time, carry less payload, use props with more pitch or diameter if the motors and ESCs can handle the current , keep a larger battery reserve. {{diagram:chart-density-altitude Maximum thrust and hover power versus density altitude ISA : at 3000 m thrust is ~74 %, hover power ~116 %.}} Cold and batteries - The internal resistance of lithium cells rises several-fold in the cold: under load the voltage sags more, the flight controller sees “low voltage” earlier, and the capacity actually delivered drops. - Rules: keep the batteries warm inside pocket, insulated bag, hand warmer at 20–25 °C before takeoff; for the first 30–60 s hover at low throttle while the cells warm up from their own current; do not lower the voltage warning threshold “so it stops beeping”; plan flight time 20–30 % shorter than in summer. - Do not charge LiPo cold below ~5–10 °C — lithium plates onto the anode, the cell degrades and becomes dangerous. - Mechanics and electronics: thickened grease, brittle plastic, condensation when you bring a cold aircraft into the warmth — let it warm up in a closed case before powering it on. Icing - Conditions: visible moisture fog, drizzle, clouds, wet snow and a temperature of roughly +2 to −10 °C; the most dangerous is supercooled drizzle and fog around 0 °C. - Ice on the props builds up within minutes: thrust drops, vibration rises, the props become unbalanced; on a plane, the stall speed rises. Small UAVs without ice protection systems do not fly in these conditions. - What to look for in a report: a temperature/dew point spread of 0–2 °C at a temperature below or near zero — fog and icing are likely. Reports: METAR and TAF METAR is the actual weather at an airfield, TAF is the forecast. An example report: text METAR XXXX 081230Z 27012G22KT 9999 BKN015 04/01 Q1013 - 27012G22KT — wind from 270° westerly , 12 knots, gusts 22 knots 1 knot ≈ 0.51 m/s: 6 m/s, gusts 11 m/s ; - 9999 — visibility 10 km or more; BKN015 — broken clouds, base at 1500 feet ~450 m ; - 04/01 — temperature +4 °C, dew point +1 °C a 3 °C spread — humid, cold, fog possible toward evening ; - Q1013 — QNH pressure 1013 hPa for barometric altitude . The wind at flight altitude comes from a winds-aloft forecast weather services with a breakdown by level, or the wind at 925 hPa ≈ 750 m and, above all, from an anemometer at the site. The “go / no-go” sheet Numbers set in advance, not on the spot: the gust limit for the aircraft, the minimum battery temperature at takeoff, the minimum temperature/dew point spread, visibility visual line of sight — per your country's rules , precipitation — none. The decision is made before you leave

text: summary Most crashes happen not because of the firmware but because of organization: nobody checked the neighbors' frequencies, nobody agreed on who watches the aircraft, there was no plan for link loss. This module is about operations as a discipline: sortie planning, team roles, frequencies and communication, pre-flight and post-flight protocol, actions during an incident and searching for a crashed aircraft. It's based on the practice of several pilots working at the same site. theory Sortie planning Before you head out, you know: the site and zones the rules module , the weather wind at altitude, precipitation, temperature — cold cuts LiPo capacity , the goal of the sortie and success criteria, who takes part and in which roles, which frequencies the neighbors occupy. Roles Even with two people it's worth naming the roles explicitly: - Pilot — flies, and does nothing else. - Observer spotter — watches the aircraft with their own eyes and the surroundings: people, birds, other aircraft; talks to the pilot without distracting them. - Technician / GCS — telemetry, parameters, logs, battery swaps, timer. - Lead — decides “go / no-go”, keeps the log. One person can combine roles, but a pilot in flight is only a pilot. Frequencies and communication - Video : a table of occupied channels at the site; spacing from neighbors rule of thumb ≥ ~37 MHz for analog ; channel changes follow the algorithm from the VTX module, on one aircraft first. - RC : the binding phrase is unique; packet rate fits the task; with several ELRS radios — different phrases, otherwise the hopping patterns will coincide. - Voice : short standard phrases: “arm”, “takeoff”, “link”, “low battery”, “landing”, “emergency”. The pilot confirms with one word. Protocols Pre-flight from the safety module, extended : frequencies coordinated, roles named, battery voltage recorded, failsafe tested on this aircraft, timer started on arming. Post-flight : disarm, battery unplugged, motor temperature, inspection of props and frame, log entry time, battery before/after, remarks , log file saved if it was a test sortie. Incidents - Link loss : the pilot calls it out, everyone watches the aircraft, nobody runs. The aircraft does what failsafe is configured to do — that's exactly why failsafe is tested in advance. - Crash : location from the last telemetry/video, the buzzer BEEPER , GPS coordinates from the GCS log. Approaching a crashed aircraft — the battery may be damaged: don't touch it if hot/puffed, don't charge it. - Injury : first aid, emergency services, then everything else. - Debrief : what happened, from the log, without looking for someone to blame; the conclusion goes into the logbook and the checklist. {{diagram:crash-search-flow Поиск начинается в первую минуту на месте: последняя точка по самому точному источнику плюс поправка на инерцию, затем схема поиска и решение старшего через 30–40 минут, пока АКБ не села.}} Case The working channel E5 5885 MHz turned out to be occupied by a crashed aircraft that kept transmitting until the end of the shift. Solution: F1 5740 MHz was chosen as the nearest free frequency, taking into account the channels of two neighbors; the switch was made first on two transmitters and a few drones as a test, then on all of them. The main lesson: the site's table of occupied frequencies must exist before the incident. Standard radio communication protocol team of 2–4 people Event Phrase Response --- --- --- Ready to arm “Aircraft 1, arm?” “Clear to arm” / “Stop, <reason ” Takeoff “Taking off” “Visual” observer Mode change “Loiter” / “Auto” “Copy” Problem “Attention, <what ” “Land” / “Continue” lead Low battery “Battery 3.5” “Return” Video/link loss “No video” / “Failsafe” “Everyone watch, don't move” Landing “Landing” “Clear” site is clear Disarm “Disarmed” “Copy, next” Short, always the same, no jargon; a newcomer learns the phrases before the first field trip. Briefing and debriefing 10 minutes each Briefing: goal of the sortie, roles, site and zones, frequencies, weather, emergency actions, who makes the “stop” call. Debriefing: what worked, what didn't, incidents and “almost-incidents” near misses — the main source of improvements , changes to the protocol/checklist, tasks for the next field trip. It gets written into the site log, not kept in someone's head. Site checklist one page Access and parking; takeoff point level, no grass in the props ; flight zone per the rules module “Rules” ; obstacles power lines, towers, trees with heights; people/animals/roads; wind anemometer or forecast by altitude , precipitation, temperature LiPo < 10 °C — warm it up ; communication phone, radios ; first aid kit, extinguisher/sand, water; table of participants' frequencies; a “where it falls on DROP” diagram for every point of the route. Worked example: an RTH test sortie Briefing: goal — test RTH on a 7" at 100 m from home; pilot — A, observer — B, technician/GCS — C; a site with a no-fly direction toward the road; wind 4 m/s from the west — RTH is into the wind, the aircraft will return slower battery margin ; frequencies: R1 analog, ELRS 2.4 250 Hz. Execution: arm by the phrases, hover at 1 m → climb to 30 m → fly out 100 m downwind → “RTH” on the switch → the observer tracks it visually → return → hover over home → manual landing. Debriefing: RTH climbed to 60 m as configured, returned in 25 s, landed manually; near miss — the observer got distracted by their phone for 5 s → into the protocol: phones on “do not disturb” for everyone except the technician. {{diagram:sortie-flow A sortie as a process: plan, briefing, site checklist, flight with assigned roles, debriefing and a log entry.}} practice Step 1. Site map A diagram: takeoff/landing point, flight zone, no-fly directions people, road, wires , team position, landing approach. Neighbors' frequencies in a table. Step 2. A one-page protocol Print it: roles, standard phrases, pre-flight and post-flight checklists, incident actions, phone numbers. Step 3.

text: summary Engineers learn from other people's crashes — if those crashes have been analyzed. This module takes three public investigations by government boards — the Matternet M2 in Zurich 2019, ArduCopter-based platform, failure due to vibration and EKF , the Alauda Airspeeder Mk II at Goodwood 2019, link loss and a kill switch that didn't work and the Freefly Alta X in Henley 2022, battery depletion — and breaks down each one using the same scheme: symptom → cause → what you see in the log → consequences → what to change in configuration and procedures. Each case ends with a line for your checklist. theory The analysis scheme Board reports AAIB in the UK, STSB/SUST in Switzerland, NTSB in the USA are written with the same logic, and that logic is your tool too: 1. Symptom — what the operator saw. 2. Sequence — events in time order from logs and telemetry. 3. Cause — technical what failed and systemic why it was possible . 4. What you see in the data — specific log messages, parameters, values. 5. Consequences — impact energy, who was nearby, what about the zone. 6. Fix — configuration, design, procedure. Distinguish three types of causes: hardware failure a part broke , configuration error a parameter didn't fit the task , operator error a procedure wasn't followed . In real crashes all three are almost always present. Case 1. Matternet M2, Zurich, May 9, 2019 STSB, final report No. 2390, aircraft SUI-9903 Context. A Swiss Post delivery quadcopter on a modified ArduCopter based on 3.5.0-rc5 , three IMUs, a flight termination system FTS with a parachute. Return flight without payload. Sequence. Takeoff at 10:37:35. After ~50 s, vibration rose on all three IMUs accelerations in places 30 m/s² , and IMU3 produced sharp deviations while IMU1 and IMU2 showed consistent values; the aircraft started oscillating in pitch. At 10:38:46 the log shows EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; the error handler activated the FTS at ~185 m above the takeoff point ~100 m above ground : all four motors stopped, the parachute deployed. The parachute line snapped at its attachment on the aircraft; uncontrolled fall, destroyed at 10:38:48. The site: a forest, ~50 m from a group of children with their teachers, who didn't hear the warning signal. Causes. Technical: increasing vibration of undetermined origin probably a resonance from an external factor — prop damage or a bird strike combined with insufficient robustness of the firmware against such an event. Systemic: the modified ArduCopter could run only two EKF lanes, EK2_IMU_MASK = 5 IMU1 and IMU3, without IMU2 — the faulty sensor couldn't be isolated; the FTS triggered an uncontrolled descent right away instead of attempting a controlled flight termination. The parachute line had been damaged by a sharp edge of the aluminum attachment even before deployment and didn't survive the jerk. What you see in the log. VIBE rises on all IMUs, but the data of one IMU diverges sharply from the other two a sign of a local source or sensor, not the frame as a whole ; EKF innovations grow → EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; switch to the FTS. Consequences. Impact energy ≈ 118 J without payload above the 80 J accepted as the threshold for serious injury . The delivery program was suspended. Seven safety recommendations. Fixes the real ones . EK2_IMU_MASK = 3 two healthy IMUs + the ability to isolate , checking both EKF lanes at arming, a second safety line and a redesigned attachment, a 100 dB siren, a log analysis tool, parachute compliance with ASTM F3322, maximum speed reduced from 20 to 16 m/s. Board recommendation No. 591: pursue a redundant propulsion concept the analysis noted that layouts with 6 or more motors have a significantly lower probability of failure . Line for your checklist: “Per-IMU vibration in the log checked after every mechanical change; behavior on EKF failsafe known and tested in SITL”. Case 2. Alauda Airspeeder Mk II, Goodwood, July 4, 2019 AAIB, report 03/2021 Context. A 95 kg demonstration multirotor, an in-house flight controller with two IMUs, no GNSS and no RTH, controlled with a FrSky Taranis X9D radio + an R9M module on 915 MHz 10 mW, FCC mode — a band not permitted for airborne use in the UK . A separate kill switch on 433 MHz LoRa with its own battery, cutting the controller's power through a relay. Sequence. ~65 s after takeoff — a sudden uncommanded transition to level attitude, then link loss. On link loss the controller froze the last throttle commands and held level — the aircraft kept climbing at ~2000 ft/min while rotating at ~40°/s for 4 min 12 s up to ~7900 ft, and entered the controlled airspace of a Gatwick holding area. On the “kill” command the observer activated the switch — with no effect. After the battery was depleted, the aircraft flipped over and fell at ~4500 ft/min into a field 40 m from houses, 700 m outside the authorized area. Impact energy ≈ 24,800 J. No injuries. Causes. The exact cause of the link loss was not determined: there was no onboard recording , the boards were destroyed. Systemic causes found by the board: the link-loss failsafe was designed as “hold throttle” rather than “descend/land”; the kill switch had no feedback loss of its channel wasn't detected , with a relay in the normally closed state a switch failure goes unnoticed until the moment you need it , on a breadboard with jumper wires, activated by a voice command instead of automatically; in the wreckage the relay and the power wire were disconnected from the board. The aircraft was not designed or tested to any standard: mounting with Velcro and zip ties, Ethernet cables as ESC signal lines, soldering with jumpers, a 42–58 V battery with no protection at all; no vibration tests, no RF tests. Speed in flight up to 25 m/s against a declared limit of 11 m/s. What you see in the data. Nothing — and that's the main lesson: without a log an investigation ends with the words “not determined”. Fixes. 15 recommendations to the regulator and the operator. For you: failsafe

summary: A hobbyist fixes the aircraft after a crash; an operator never lets it get to a crash. The difference is the logbook and the inspection schedule: every flight is recorded, every battery has a history of its cell resistance, props are replaced by a rule rather than “when they crack”, and trends in vi
headings: Logbooks Battery service life Inspection schedule Logs as a maintenance tool Reliability: numbers instead of feelings One-page FMEA Step 1. Logbooks Step 2. Batteries Step 3. Trend from logs Step 4. Schedule and FMEA
text: summary A hobbyist fixes the aircraft after a crash; an operator never lets it get to a crash. The difference is the logbook and the inspection schedule: every flight is recorded, every battery has a history of its cell resistance, props are replaced by a rule rather than “when they crack”, and trends in vibration and motor balance from the logs warn you about wear before it turns into a failure. This module covers aircraft and battery logbooks, battery retirement criteria, an inspection schedule based on flight hours, log analysis as a maintenance tool, and reliability basics — failure rate, MTBF, series and redundant systems — with a calculation that shows why six motors instead of four. theory Logbooks - Aircraft logbook : date, pilot, site, task, flight time min , battery, remarks, link to the log; separately, repairs and replacements what, why, serial numbers . The total flight time of the aircraft and its components motors, ESCs, props is the basis of the inspection schedule. - Battery logbook : battery number sticker , purchase date, cycles, voltage before/after the flight, internal resistance of the cells by date, damage. A number on the battery is mandatory — otherwise the “bad battery” is impossible to pin down. - Format : a spreadsheet or CSV in git next to the aircraft parameters module “Configs in CI” — you get history and search for free. Battery service life - Internal resistance IR of each cell is the main indicator. Measure it with a charger that has an IR function compare using the same device at the same temperature . Rising IR means less output under load and more heating. - Retirement criteria guidelines, check with the manufacturer : cell IR has grown to roughly 1.5–2 times the new value; cell imbalance after charging and resting is more than ~0.03–0.05 V; puffing; capacity below ~80 % of rated; mechanical damage after a crash. A puffed or damaged battery: discharge it and dispose of it properly, do not fly it. - Storage : 3.80–3.85 V per cell storage , cool, in a fireproof bag or box; do not keep them fully charged for more than a few days. - Operating practice : do not discharge below the landing threshold module “Power” , do not charge them hot or cold, use balance charging. Inspection schedule When What Criterion --- --- --- Before every flight props, prop and motor mounting, battery and connector, antennas, straps cracks and chips, play, connector heating After every flight motor and ESC temperature by touch, props, frame, logbook entry one motor noticeably hotter than the others — take it apart After any impact props all of them, not only the broken one , frame, motors for play and binding, check calibrations a prop that touched something — replace it Every ~10–20 h motor bearings spin by hand — grinding, play , frame screws, soldering and connectors, flight controller dampers grinding and play — replace the bearings or the motor Every ~50 h or per season full teardown: wiring, insulation, power connectors, planned firmware update signs of heating, chafing The intervals are starting values; your own come from the logbook: if bearings die within 30 h, the schedule is 20. {{diagram:maint-inspection-timeline Регламент по налёту: проверки перед и после каждого полёта и после удара идут всегда, плановые — по часам, а интервал подшипников подгоняется по журналу умирают за 30 ч — осмотр каждые 20 ч .}} {{diagram:post-crash-recheck-flow После аварии порядок важен: АКБ первой и в карантин, затем механика и проводка, затем проверка без пропов — и только потом новые пропы и контрольное висение.}} Logs as a maintenance tool A log is not only “why it crashed” but also “what is wearing out”: - Vibration VIBE in ArduPilot, gyro in Betaflight Blackbox : growth from flight to flight with the same props — bearings, a prop, a loose mount. - Motor balance RCOU / motor n : one motor consistently higher than the others in hover — it is weaker wear, prop or the aircraft is out of balance. - Compass MAG : increased current-induced interference after wiring repairs. - Battery BAT : voltage sag at the same current grows — the battery resistance is growing. A trend matters more than a single value: one point is noise, five points are wear. Reliability: numbers instead of feelings - Failure rate λ — failures per hour roughly constant during normal operation . MTBF = 1/λ — mean time between failures. An MTBF of 1000 h does not mean “1000 h without failures”: the probability of running t hours without a failure is R t = e^ −λt , and for 1000 h that is only 37 %. - Bathtub curve : at the start, early failures defects, cold solder joints → normal operation → wear-out. Hence acceptance testing of new aircraft ground test, first flights low and close and replacement by service life before the wear-out zone. - Series system — failure of any component = failure of the system: R = R₁·R₂·…·Rₙ. For motors, a quadcopter is a series system of four: R = r⁴. - Redundancy — the system works as long as at least one of the duplicates is alive: R = 1 − 1 − r ². A hexacopter that can make it home on five motors is “5 out of 6 needed”: R = r⁶ + 6·r⁵· 1 − r . But the ability to survive a motor failure depends on the frame, thrust-to-weight ratio and firmware — you test it, you don't assume it module “Redundancy” . - Example : motor λ = 1/1000 h illustrative . Over 100 h of flight time without replacement: quad R = e^ −0.4 ≈ 0.67, a hexa that survives one failure ≈ 0.90. The same calculation shows why replacing motors by service life raises reliability more than it seems. {{diagram:chart-reliability Probability of avoiding a loss due to motor failure versus flight time: a quad needs all four versus a hexa that survives one failure.}} One-page FMEA For each component: how it can fail → what the pilot will see → what the aircraft will do → how to detect it in advance → what we do. Five rows for the motor, ESC, battery, receiver and GNSS give you a plan of the inspections and checks that actually matter. practice

text: summary Troubleshooting is not a string of guesses but the elimination of branches of a tree, where every step is confirmed by a fact: a multimeter reading, a firmware message, a log line. This module gives you a tree for five typical situations — “won't arm,” “motors don't spin or spin wrong,” “goes crazy on throttle,” “ESC/board burns when you plug in the battery,” “loses link or video” — and a rule for adding your own cases to it. Tools: smoke stopper, multimeter, CLI status /pre-arm messages, Blackbox/DataFlash. theory Troubleshooting rules 1. Fact first, hypothesis second. The firmware almost always tells you what's wrong: Betaflight — status in the CLI the Arming disable flags line , INAV — the Status tab and status in the CLI, ArduPilot — PreArm messages in the GCS. Start there, not with resoldering. 2. One change — one test. If you changed two parameters and it started working, you don't know which one helped, and you don't know what you broke. 3. From cheap to expensive. Visual inspection and the multimeter come before the oscilloscope and replacing the board. 4. Safety at every step. Props off for anything involving the motors. The first power-up after any soldering goes through a smoke stopper. 5. Write down the path. Steps with their results go into a note; the cause you found goes into the tree and into the vehicle's log. Tree 1. Won't arm Read the reason: Betaflight CLI → status → Arming disable flags: ... . The CLI prints short names from runtime_config.c FAILSAFE, CALIB, NO_ACC_CAL, CMS, BOOTGRACE, MOTOR_PROTO, DSHOT_TELEM, ARMSWITCH in 4.5 / ARM_SWITCH in 2025.12+ ; below, some flags are named as in the documentation. The most common ones: - RXLOSS / RX_FAILSAFE — the receiver isn't delivering channels. → Port and protocol UART, CRSF/SBUS, inversion for SBUS on F4 , bind, receiver power 5 V with a multimeter , the Receiver tab — do the channels move? - THROTTLE — throttle is above minimum. → Stick calibration in the radio, min_check , channel reversal. - ANGLE — the vehicle is tilted more than small_angle . → The surface, accelerometer calibration. - CALIBRATING / ACC_CALIBRATION / NOGYRO — the gyro isn't calibrated or isn't detected. → Keep it still at power-up; NOGYRO — a hardware problem or the wrong firmware target. - ARM_SWITCH — the arm switch was on when power was applied. → Switch it off, then on. - MSP / CLI / CMS_MENU — the configurator is connected or the OSD menu is open. → Unplug USB, exit the menu. - NOPREARM — a prearm mode is configured but not activated. - DSHOT_TELEM before 4.5 — RPMFILTER — the RPM filter is enabled but there's no ESC telemetry bidirectional DShot isn't supported by the ESC firmware or isn't enabled . - BOOT_GRACE_TIME — just wait a few seconds after power-up. - MOTOR_PROTOCOL — no motor protocol selected. INAV: the Status tab shows the reasons Navigation is unsafe, Compass not calibrated, Hardware failure... . ArduPilot: PreArm: ... in the GCS — each line names the culprit Compass not calibrated, Gyros inconsistent, RC not calibrated, Throttle below failsafe, GPS: No Fix, Battery failsafe, etc. ; don't disable the checks in ARMING_SKIPCHK before 4.7 — ARMING_CHECK — fix the cause. {{diagram:arming-tree Tree 1 as a diagram: flag → cause → check.}} Tree 2. Motors don't spin / spin wrong Props off. - No motor responds in the Motors tab. → Does the protocol DShot300/600 and motor_pwm_protocol match the ESC? → Are the ESCs getting power voltage at the pads ? → Are the signal wires on the right pads resource MOTOR ? → Do the ESCs beep when power is applied startup tune ? If not, the ESC is dead or has no power. - One motor doesn't spin, the others do. → Swap its signal wire with a working one: if the problem moved with the wire — it's the signal/FC pad; if it stayed — it's the ESC or the motor. → Is the resistance of all three motor phases the same? → Phase solder joints a cold joint is typical . - The motor twitches but won't start. → Lost contact on one phase solder joint, chafed wire or a damaged ESC. → Continuity-test the phases, wiggle them. - Spinning the wrong way / wrong order. → Motors tab: check the number and direction of each one against the frame diagram; change the direction in the ESC firmware BLHeli Suite/Configurator or by swapping two phases. The “props in/out” direction must be consistent across all four. - The drone flips over on takeoff. → This is Tree 2: order/direction or the wrong mixer mixer isn't for your frame . Tree 3. “Goes crazy” on throttle Symptom: it hovers fine, shakes above 60–70% throttle, motors are hot, the drone behaves unpredictably. - Do you have a Blackbox log? If not, record one; otherwise you're guessing. Gyro spectrum: a huge peak at the motor frequency → mechanics imbalance, props, motor bearing play ; wideband noise that grows with throttle → vibration + insufficient filtering; a peak that doesn't move with throttle → frame resonance. - Gyro noise grew after a replacement/repair? → Is there a capacitor on the power bus? Its lead solder joints, its capacitance. → FC mounting dampers, taut wires . - ESC desync a motor suddenly loses RPM, a jerk, then it recovers; in the log — an eRPM dip on one motor : → ESC settings timing, demag , DShot too fast for long wires, a damaged motor; drop the protocol to DShot300, check the phases. - Voltage sag: in the log VBAT drops below the threshold under throttle → the BEC reboots the FC instant loss of control or the ESCs go into protection. → Connector, battery, solder joints. - PID/filters : too much D or P with insufficient filtering → oscillations at high throttle, where there's more noise. → Filters based on the spectrum, then reduce D. - Interference on the receiver from the VTX at full power LQ drops with throttle — rare, but it happens with ripple on the VTX supply : → a VTX power filter, spacing the antennas apart. Tree 4. Something burns/smokes when you plug in the battery Disconnect immediately. From here on — only through a smoke stopper a bulb/lim

text: summary Картинка в очках — это канал управления, а не съёмка: аналоговый DVR пишет кадр стандартной чёткости с помехами, цифровой — то, что дошло по радио. Для ролика нужна отдельная запись: экшн-камера или запись на борту цифрового видеомодуля. Модуль разбирает классы камер с массой и ценой этой массы во времени полёта, стабилизацию в камере и в Gyroflow гироскоп камеры или Blackbox полётника , экспозицию через угол затвора и ND-фильтры со счётом стопов, вибрации и «желе», наклон камеры против скорости, DVR для разбора аварий и поиска, карты памяти и питание камеры. После модуля ты выбираешь камеру, фильтр и настройки под задачу и находишь причину дефекта по описанию кадра. Практика расчётная: экспозиция, объём записи, геометрия наклона и разбор четырёх дефектов. theory Три записи и зачем каждая Запись Где пишется Что в ней Для чего --- --- --- --- DVR очков аналог SD-карта очков или модуля приёмника кадр PAL 576 / NTSC 480 строк после радио: снег, срывы, OSD разбор полёта, поиск: последний кадр и координаты в OSD DVR очков цифра очки HDZero — только так; DJI O4 — по настройке Record With то, что дошло по радио, с OSD то же; видно, где деградировал линк Запись на борту видеомодуля память или microSD модуля DJI O3/O4, Walksnail кадр с камеры без радиопотерь, без OSD разбор аварий, ролик среднего качества Экшн-камера своя microSD 4K, 10 бит у старших моделей, гироскоп для Gyroflow ролик Главное следствие: бортовая запись остаётся на борту. Если аппарат потерян, искать его помогает только то, что записано в очках и на пульте ops-field . Порядок включения, нагрев и запись по системам — в bf-hd-osd-video , сравнение систем — в link-digital-video . Классы камер и что они стоят аппарату Масса камеры — это время полёта и тюн. Оценка по теории диска f-aero-props : мощность висения растёт как m^1.5, значит при той же батарее время висения t ∝ m^−1.5. Для 5" массой 600 г без камеры: Класс Пример масса по производителю Цена, на ноябрь 2026 Гироскоп для Gyroflow Время висения, доля от «без камеры» --- --- --- --- --- Полноразмерная экшн-камера GoPro HERO13 Black 159 г с батареей; DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro 146 г ~300–500 $ оценка, не проверено да HERO 8+ даже с HyperSmooth; DJI — EIS выкл. 0.70 +159 г 360° Insta360 X5 200 г, 8K30, до 180 Мбит/с не проверено нет 360° Gyroflow не поддерживает; стабилизация в приложении производителя 0.65 +200 г «Голая» GoPro корпус снят, питание от полётной АКБ Flywoo Naked V1/V2 на базе HERO9–12: 45/49 г; GoPro HERO10 Bones 54 г, 5–27 В 350–590 $ Flywoo, обзор Oscar Liang да — та же электроника 0.90 +45 г Лёгкая FPV-камера RunCam Thumb 2 27.8 г, 4K60 100 Мбит/с, только 5 В, до 0.7 А ~99 $ обзор да, отдельный файл .gcsv 0.93 +28 г Мини-камера на магните Insta360 GO 3S 39.1 г, 4K30, 120 Мбит/с не проверено да 0.91 +39 г Запись на борту видеомодуля DJI O4 Pro ≈32 г камера + модуль , 4K120, 130 Мбит/с; O4 ≈8.2 г, 4K60, 100 Мбит/с; Walksnail HD Pro 1080p60, 32 ГБ встроенной памяти O4 Pro 229 $ Adorama, 22.11.2026 ; Walksnail HD Pro kit 159 $ caddxfpv да, но камера O3/O4 должна стоять на мягком креплении или нужна Optical correction заменяет FPV-камеру и VTX, добавки почти нет Масса — не только время. Камера сверху спереди поднимает и сдвигает вперёд центр масс и увеличивает момент инерции по тангажу: тот же PID даёт другую реакцию, а моторы задней пары разгружаются. После установки тяжёлой камеры снимают Blackbox и проверяют тюн bf-pid , bf-blackbox — так же, как после смены батареи. Для «голой» GoPro теряется защита корпуса и встроенная батарея нужна для обновления прошивки , а перегрев — частая жалоба на такие сборки по обзору Flywoo V2 металл спереди помогает . Стабилизация: в камере или в Gyroflow В камере HyperSmooth у GoPro, RockSteady у DJI — электронная: кадр кадрируется и сдвигается по гироскопу в реальном времени. Плюсы: готовый файл. Ограничения: кроп выбран навсегда, алгоритм видит только прошлое, горизонт держится не во всех режимах у Osmo Action 5 Pro HorizonSteady — только 1080p/2.7K до 60 кадр/с, HorizonBalancing — до 4K 60 кадр/с; у HERO13 Black Horizon Leveling в камере — не во всех режимах . Резкие флипы FPV и вибрации — худший случай для любого EIS. Gyroflow GPLv3, Windows/Linux/macOS/Android/iOS, плагины для DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, Final Cut стабилизирует после полёта по записанному гироскопу. Что ему нужно: - Данные движения. Гироскоп камеры в файле GoPro HERO 5+ — но HERO5 и HERO7 помечены «Bad on FPV drone»; HERO 8+ можно снимать с HyperSmooth; DJI Avata/O3/O4/Action 4–6 — EIS выключен и FOV Wide, иначе гироскоп не пишется; Insta360 GO/Ace — у части моделей режим FreeFrame или внешний лог: Blackbox Betaflight/INAV .bbl , .bfl , .csv и логи ArduPilot .bin , .log . Нет гироскопа — Optical correction с 1.7.0 оценивает движение по пикселям, хуже. - Профиль линзы. Встроенные официальные профили для GoPro, DJI, Sony, Insta360, RunCam Thumb/5 Orange; HERO11+ пишет калибровку в файл. Для своей камеры — калибровка по шахматке. - Синхронизация. Для гироскопа камеры GoPro 8+, DJI, Insta360 не нужна. Для лога полётника — нужна: Gyroflow сравнивает движение из лога с оптическим потоком видео; обычно хватает 2–3 точек на участках с движением по всем осям, у всех точек смещения должны быть близки. - Наклон камеры. Для лога полётника гироскоп стоит в осях рамы, а камера наклонена: угол вводят в Motion data → Rotation → Pitch вверх — плюс, 30° → 30 . Ошибка в несколько градусов даёт дрейф и «качание» горизонта. - Rolling shutter. Нужна величина Frame readout time; для GoPro, DJI, Insta360, Sony она подставляется сама. Смена значения требует пересинхронизации. - Сглаживание и горизонт. Алгоритм Default подходит в 99.5 % случаев по документации; Smoothness 0–1, по умолчанию 0.5; Horizon lock держит горизонт и требует большего кропа; FOV 1.0 с Dynamic zoom использует максимум пикселей. Порядок работы: загрузить видео → проверить профиль линзы → данные движения из файла или лог FC → наклон → синхронизация → сглаживание, горизонт → экспорт или проект в монтажке через плаг

title: Onboard power circuit design
summary: An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and len
headings: Load map Linear vs switching BEC Sag and internal resistance Ripple and the capacitor Protection Wire gauges Step 1. Power tree Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges Step 3. Capacitor Step 4. Protection Step 5. Measure (link to the measurements module)
text: summary An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and length, understand where sags and ripple come from and why a low-ESR capacitor on the bus isn't an option but part of the circuit. Separately — protection: smoke stopper, fuse, reverse polarity. theory Load map Before choosing components, draw the power tree: battery → power bus → ESC ×4…8, 5 V BEC, 9–12 V BEC → loads. Typical currents: {{diagram:power-tree Power tree: from the battery to the power bus and separate BECs; each load with its own current.}} Load Voltage Typical current --- --- --- FC + gyro 5 V 3.3 internal 0.1–0.2 A ELRS receiver 5 V 0.1–0.3 A on-board TX module up to 0.5 GPS with compass 5 V 3.3 0.05–0.1 A Digital video system air unit 9–12 V 0.5–1.2 A, higher peaks Analog VTX 800 mW–1 W 9–12 V / 5 V 0.4–0.7 A Servos wing 5–6 V / 7.4 V 0.5–1 A each while moving Companion Pi 4/5 5 V 1–3 A, peaks up to 5 Lighting/LEDs 5 V 0.06 A per LED Add them up with a 50% margin: a 5 V BEC on an aircraft with GPS, receiver and FC and no companion — 1 A is enough; with a Raspberry you need a separate 3–5 A BEC. Linear vs switching BEC - Linear LDO — dumps the excess voltage as heat: at 6S 25 V → 5 V and 0.5 A it dissipates 10 W. Unsuitable for high voltages and currents, but has no ripple — good for the gyro and RF. - Switching buck — 85–95% efficiency, but produces ripple at the switching frequency hundreds of kHz and its harmonics; a bad buck next to the receiver means lost LQ. Flight controllers have a filtered 5 V / 9 V buck. - A good trick: buck down to 5.5–6 V, then an LDO to 5 V for the sensitive part many FCs are built this way: 3.3 V for the gyro through an LDO . Sag and internal resistance Voltage under load U = E − I·R_int. R_int of a 6S 4P Li-Ion battery ≈ 20–40 mΩ per cell → 30–60 mΩ per pack R × 6 / 4 ; at 60 A the sag is 1.8–3.6 V. Plus the wires: 12 AWG ≈ 5.2 mΩ/m, 14 AWG ≈ 8.3, 16 AWG ≈ 13.2. 20 cm out and back of 14 AWG at 60 A is 0.2 V, which is small; but an XT60 connector with oxidized contacts can add more. The sag isn't dangerous in itself, but because the BEC on the flight controller gets an input voltage below its threshold some bucks shut off below 7–8 V on 2S — an FC reboot in flight. Ripple and the capacitor ESCs switch the windings at tens of kHz, and the current in the battery wires jerks. The inductance of the wires L ≈1 µH per meter turns dI/dt into voltage spikes: U = L·dI/dt. These are ripple and spikes on the power bus that pass into the FC supply, into the gyro noise in the log and into the video lines . The fix is a low-ESR electrolytic or polymer capacitor right on the ESC/PDB power pads: 470–1000 µF at 35 V for 4S, 1000 µF at 50 V for 6S ≥ 30% voltage margin . It acts as a local source: it delivers energy on the edge and absorbs the spike. Short leads — otherwise the lead inductance spoils the effect. Protection - Smoke stopper — a bulb or a resistor/current limiter in series with the positive lead at the first power-up. A short circuit — the bulb lights up, the aircraft doesn't smoke. - Fuse — on large aircraft on the power bus not on the motors — the current is too high and pulsed and on the companion bus. - Reverse polarity — XT60/XT30 protect by their shape, but soldering one backwards kills the board in a second. A Schottky diode in series 0.3–0.5 V drop or a P-MOSFET ideal diode for low-voltage branches. - Connectors : XT30 up to ~15–30 A continuous, XT60 ~30 A continuous briefly up to ~60 A , XT90 ~45 A continuous; AS150/XT150 for high currents. A connector overloaded for its current rated below the real current heats up, a hot one oxidizes, an oxidized one heats up even more. Wire gauges {{widget:wire-drop}} Rule of thumb for short runs on board: 12 AWG up to ~60–80 A, 14 AWG up to ~40–50 A, 16 AWG up to ~25 A, 18 AWG up to ~15 A, 20–22 AWG — signal and 5 V branches up to 2–3 A. The criteria are insulation heating and the acceptable drop; long wires on a wing — one size up. practice Step 1. Power tree Draw the tree for your build with the current on each branch from the table and datasheets . The 5 V total and the 9–12 V total — separately. Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges For each branch: BEC type buck/LDO , rating ≥ 1.5 × the total, input voltage with margin for a fully charged 6S 25.2 V . Wire gauge — from the table. Step 3. Capacitor Choose the capacitance and voltage, solder it to the ESC/PDB pads with leads no longer than 10–15 mm. Record a hover log before/after: gyro noise in the band above 300 Hz spectrum should drop. Step 4. Protection A smoke stopper at every first power-up after soldering. Check with a multimeter that there's no short between + and − before connecting the battery the resistance shouldn't be below hundreds of ohms; with a capacitor it rises at first . Step 5. Measure link to the measurements module Sag under load: battery voltage with no load and in hover from the log . 5 V ripple — with an oscilloscope with AC coupling: typically < 50–100 mV p-p. diagnostics - Symptom: the FC reboots on a sharp throttle punch - Possible cause: a sag below the BEC threshold or a bad connector contact. - What to do: VBAT log, check the XT connector, the capacitor, a higher-capacity/fresher battery. - Symptom: lines in the analog video on throttle - Possible cause: power bus ripple gets into the VTX. - What to do: a capacitor on the power bus, power the VTX from a filtered BEC, an LC filter. - Symptom: gyro noise went up after replacing the ESC - Possible cause: a different switching frequency, no capacitor. - What to do: a capacitor on the pads, check the FC grounding. - Symptom: the BEC is hot - Possible cause: a linear BEC with a high input voltage, or current above the rating. - What to do: recompute the dissipated power, a

summary: What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. headings: Multimeter Oscilloscope DShot on the oscilloscope Logic analyzer Measurement safety Step 1. Map of measurement points Step 2. Sag under load Step 3. BEC ripple Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Step 5. Report A decoded DShot frame What you should get and what to record
text: summary What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. This module is about three instruments: the multimeter voltage, current, continuity, resistance , the oscilloscope sags, ripple, PWM/DShot waveforms, noise and the logic analyzer decoding UART, I2C, SPI, DShot . What to measure, how to connect, how not to fry the instrument or the aircraft, and how to read the result. theory Multimeter - Voltage — in parallel with the load. Useful: the voltage of each battery cell balance , 5 V and 9 V on the BEC under load. - Continuity — before applying power: + to − on the power bus, 5 V to GND. A beep = a short. With a capacitor the resistance rises as it charges — that's normal. - Current — in series, through the 10 A jack; anything more — only with a clamp meter or through the FC current sensor. Never measure voltage in current mode: that's a short circuit through the meter. - Resistance — checking motor windings three identical values of a few tenths of an ohm , a broken wire. - Limitation: a multimeter shows the average/RMS; it doesn't see brief sags and ripple. Oscilloscope Shows voltage over time. For on-board work 2 channels and 50–100 MHz are enough; a USB oscilloscope will do too. - Sag : a channel on the power bus, timebase 100 ms/div, trigger on the falling edge; punch the throttle — you see the depth and duration of the dip. - Ripple : AC coupling removes the DC component , 20–50 mV/div, timebase 10–50 µs/div — you see the ESC/BEC switching frequency and the p-p amplitude. Measure with a short ground spring instead of the long alligator clip — otherwise you pick up noise from the probe itself. - Signals : PWM servos — a 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms 50 Hz ; UART — bursts of bits with idle at the high level; DShot — bursts of 16 pulses of different widths. - A ×10 probe reduces the load on the circuit and extends the bandwidth; for 3.3 V logic it's mandatory. DShot on the oscilloscope A DShot frame is 16 bits: 11 throttle bits, 1 telemetry bit, 4 CRC bits. Each bit is a pulse: “1” is long ~75% of the bit period , “0” is short ~37% . DShot600 is 600 kbit/s, a bit ≈ 1.67 µs, a frame ≈ 27 µs. On screen — a burst of 16 pulses repeating at the PID loop rate for example, every 125 µs at 8 kHz . Problems you can see: ringing on the edges long wire, no termination , a level that doesn't reach 3.3 V weak driver , dropped frames. Logic analyzer Records digital levels on many channels and decodes protocols. A cheap 8-channel 24 MHz one with software like PulseView/sigrok is enough for UART up to 1 Mbaud, I2C at 400 kHz, SPI up to a few MHz and DShot600 you need ≥ 4–5 samples per bit — 12–24 MHz is better . - UART : connect to the TX line and GND, set the baud rate 115200 for MSP, 420000 for CRSF! , the decoder shows the bytes. You can see: the wrong baud rate garbage , inversion SBUS is an inverted UART at 100000 8E2 . - I2C : SDA and SCL, the decoder shows addresses and ACK/NACK. A NACK on an address — the sensor isn't there or the address is different; no pull-up — the lines don't go high. - SPI : CLK, MOSI, MISO, CS — reading the gyro registers. - A common ground with the aircraft — always. Levels are 3.3 V; most analyzers tolerate 5 V lines, 12 V — no. Measurement safety - Props off for any measurement on ESCs/motors. - The oscilloscope ground is tied to protective earth: on a circuit that isn't referenced to earth battery powered that's fine; on a mains-powered supply you must not clip the probe ground to a point that carries a potential. - The probe never touches two pins at once: tiny FC pads are the number one way to cause a short with the instrument. {{diagram:measure-tools Which instrument for which question: values — multimeter, waveform — oscilloscope, protocol — logic analyzer.}} practice Step 1. Map of measurement points On the aircraft's schematic mark: the power bus, the 5 V output, the 9 V output, the receiver UART, DShot on one motor, the compass I2C. Find convenient pads. Step 2. Sag under load Without props the measurement is meaningless — use the log VBAT in hover or an oscilloscope on a test stand with a real load aircraft tied down, props on, short throttle pulses, extremely carefully and with an observer . Record: U with no load, U at maximum, duration of the dip. Step 3. BEC ripple AC coupling, 5 V under receiver/GPS load. Record p-p and frequency. Compare with/without a capacitor on the power bus. Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Capture a DShot frame at low throttle without props: decode the 16 bits by hand, compute the throttle value DShot 48–2047 and check the CRC. Capture CRSF between the receiver and the FC at 420000 baud: find the channels frame type 0x16 . Step 5. Report A table: point, instrument, value, normal range, conclusion. A decoded DShot frame Throttle value 1046, telemetry bit 0. Twelve bits: 10000010110 0 . CRC = v ⊕ v 4 ⊕ v 8 & 0xF = 6 0110 , where v is those 12 bits. The frame is 16 bits 1000001011000110 0x82C6 . On the oscilloscope each DShot600 bit lasts ≈ 1.67 µs: “1” is a long high pulse, “0” a short one. From your captured frame compute the value and the CRC and compare them with the throttle you set. What you should get and what to record - Sag under load: VBAT in the log in hover and at a short burst of full throttle — the difference and how it relates to the internal resistance from the “Electricity” module. - BEC ripple: the swing p-p on 5 V under load — tens of millivolts for a good BEC. Hundreds of millivolts mean interference in the video and sensor glitches. Record p-p and frequency with and without the capacitor on the power bus. - CRSF: the channels frame starts with the address byte 0xC8 , then the length 0x18 24 and the type 0x16 RC channels packed : 16 channels of 11 bits each. - Table: point, instrument, value, normal range, conclusion — one row per measurement. Without the “normal range” column a measurement tells you nothing. The lab is passed when the sag under load is measured

summary: LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration fo
headings: Three chemistries in numbers S/P configuration Spot welding BMS, balancer and the drone Internal resistance and health Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job Step 2. S/P calculation Step 3. Welding design Step 4. Pack test
text: summary LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration for current and capacity with internal resistance in mind, build a pack by spot welding nickel strip without overheating the cell, pick a BMS and balancer so they don't cut power to the aircraft in flight, and measure the real capacity and sag with a cycle under load. theory Three chemistries in numbers Parameter LiPo graphite/LCO-NMC Li-Ion 18650/21700 NMC/NCA LiFePO4 --- --- --- --- Cell nominal 3.7 V 4.2 full, 3.3–3.5 land 3.6 V 4.2 full, 2.5–3.0 land 3.2 V 3.65 full, 2.5 land Specific energy 150–200 Wh/kg 220–270 Wh/kg high-capacity 21700 90–140 Wh/kg Continuous current 20–100C a 1300 mAh 75C pack ≈ 100 A 3–10C per cell P42A: 45 A at 4.2 Ah; 40T: 35 A at 4 Ah; VTC6: 15 A per datasheet, 30 A with an 80 °C cutoff, at 3 Ah 1–3C, high-current ones up to 10C Cycle life 150–300 cycles to 80% 300–500 2000–4000 Internal resistance 1–5 mΩ/cell 15–40 mΩ/cell 5–20 mΩ 26650 Safety catches fire easily, puffs burns, but protected by the can; CID/PTC in “protected” versions very tolerant of overcharge and temperature Where it fits racing, freestyle, anything with T/W 3 long range, wings, heavy-lift, companion power ground equipment, heavy slow platforms, stationary Rule: Li-Ion wins when the average pack current is ≤ 1–2C and the flight is longer than 15 minutes. If hover needs 3C, go LiPo. S/P configuration - S sets the voltage: 6S Li-Ion = 21.6 V nominal, 25.2 full, 18 V to land 3.0 V/cell , 15 V is the absolute limit. - P sets the current and capacity: 4P of P42A = 16.8 Ah, 4 × 45 = 180 A continuous per datasheet, but in practice limited by heating and sag. - Sag : R of the pack = R of the cell × S / P. 6S4P P42A ≈ 25 mΩ × 6 / 4 ≈ 38 mΩ plus strip and connections — +10–20 mΩ . At 60 A the sag is ≈ 2.3–3.5 V — almost 1 cell “lost” under load. That's why for the same job you size Li-Ion with margin on P, not “right at the datasheet current”. - Heat : P = I²·R on the pack: 60 A × 60 A × 0.05 Ω = 180 W over the whole pack — noticeable heating in 10 minutes. Rule of thumb: average current ≤ 1.5C for 21700 without forced cooling. - Mass budget : 6S4P 21700 ≈ 24 × 70 g = 1.7 kg + strip/case ≈ 1.85 kg for 363 Wh ≈ 195 Wh/kg including hardware . Spot welding You must not solder to cells: overheating the terminal damages the separator and the protection. Weld with nickel strip: - Strip : pure nickel not nickel-plated steel — its resistance is several times higher and it rusts . A 0.15 × 8 mm cross-section carries roughly 7–10 A per path continuously; for high-current packs use 0.2 × 10 mm, “doubled” strip or a copper bus bar with a nickel layer, or parallel paths. - Welder : a capacitor/supercapacitor or transformer welder; tune it on scraps: a weld should tear the strip leaving a crater, not peel off. Two electrodes on the same side, 2–4 welds per cell. - Order : welding layout on paper → cells of equal capacity and voltage spread ≤ 0.02 V → insulator rings on the positive terminals → parallel groups → series links → balance wires from each group → heat shrink/case with air for cooling. - Safety : shorting a 21700 through nickel strip means hundreds of amps and a burn; work one connection at a time, no metal tools over the assembled part, safety glasses, sand nearby, a non-combustible box and a bucket of water for cooling class D is for metallic lithium, and Li-Ion has none . BMS, balancer and the drone A BMS protects against overcharge, overdischarge, overcurrent and temperature. For flight a classic BMS is dangerous: a discharge cutoff on current/temperature in the air = a crash. Options: 1. No BMS on board — balancing through the balance connector at charging like LiPo , voltage monitoring by the flight controller voltage failsafe . The standard for flying packs. 2. Charge-only BMS : balancer and protection while charging, discharge goes direct. Good for stationary and ground use. 3. Smart BMS with configurable thresholds JK/Jikong and similar, with a 1–2 A active balancer and Bluetooth : for ground stations and heavy slow platforms; for flight — only with discharge protection disabled and with an understanding of the consequences. An active balancer moves energy between groups is needed for large capacity and infrequent full charges; a passive one burns the excess on resistors is enough for 4–6S flying packs balanced regularly. Internal resistance and health The charger shows IR per cell: a new 21700 ≈ 15–25 mΩ; a rise to 50+ is end of life for high-current work. A difference between groups 30% means a weak group — check the welds/cells. LiPo: 1–3 mΩ new, 10+ — time to move it to ground duty. {{diagram:chemistry-choice Choosing a chemistry: LiPo when you need current, Li-Ion when you need energy, LiFePO4 when you need cycle life and safety.}} practice Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job For your aircraft: average hover/cruise current from the log, the desired flight time, the mass. Work out the C-rate for the LiPo and Li-Ion candidates. If the average current is ≤ 1.5C on Li-Ion, go on with Li-Ion. Step 2. S/P calculation Pick a cell datasheet: capacity, continuous current, IR . P ≥ maximum current / 0.6 × cell current — a 40% margin for heating and sag. Work out the pack R, the sag at maximum and in hover, the heat, the mass and Wh/kg. Compare with LiPo. Step 3. Welding design Layout: cell arrangement, strip direction, path cross-section for the group current, balance wire points, connector XT60/XT90 depending on current , an output fuse. The lab accepts “designed” without building it. Step 4. Pack test 1. Full charge with balancing, record the group voltages. 2. Discharge under constant load a discharger, a resistor, or a flight with a current log down to 3.0 V/cell: the integral of I·dt = the r
